item.title: Python Introduction
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Python is a programming language known for being easy to read and powerful at the same time. It's the most popular language for beginners, and also one of the most used by professionals: in data science, AI and machine learning, automation, web back-ends and scientific research.

Your first Python program

print("Hello, world!")
print(2 + 3)
print("Python", "is", "fun")

Output:

Hello, world!
5
Python is fun

print() shows a value on the screen. Passing several values separated by commas prints them with spaces in between. Compared with many languages, there's very little extra: no semicolons, no curly braces, no main function required.

Why Python is beginner-friendly

Here's a program that greets a list of people:

names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]

for name in names:
    if name.startswith("A"):
        print(f"Hello, {name}! Your name starts with A.")
    else:
        print(f"Hi, {name}!")

Even without knowing Python, you can probably guess what it does. That readability is Python's main design goal: code is read far more often than it's written.

Indentation is part of the language

Notice the spaces at the start of some lines. In Python, indentation defines blocks of code. The lines indented under for belong to the loop; the lines under if belong to the condition.

age = 20
if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")      # inside the if (4 spaces)
    print("Don't forget your ID.")
print("This always runs.")       # back at the left: outside the if

Other languages use { } for blocks and indentation is just style. In Python it's required, which forces everyone's code to be neatly formatted. The standard is 4 spaces per level; your editor inserts them when you press Tab.

What people build with Python

Learning Python opens all these doors, and it's the main language for working with AI.

Python is interpreted

You don't compile Python into a program file first. The Python interpreter reads your code and runs it line by line. That makes it quick to experiment: write a line, run it, see the result.

The trade-off: pure Python is slower than languages like C or Go. In practice, heavy work (maths, AI) is done by libraries written in fast languages, and Python acts as the easy-to-write "glue".

Python 3

There were two major versions: Python 2 and Python 3. Python 2 reached its end of life in 2020. Everything in this course is Python 3, and that's the only version you should learn. If an old tutorial writes print "hello" without brackets, it's Python 2.

Comments

# This is a comment. Python ignores it.
print("Comments explain why the code does something.")  # comments can go here too

Where Python runs

  • On your computer, after installing it (next lesson).
  • In the browser, with free tools like Google Colab, Replit or Programiz Online Compiler. Great for practising right now.
  • On servers, in the cloud, even on small devices like the Raspberry Pi.

Note: Python examples on VitalStack don't have a Try it Yourself button (that runs only HTML and JavaScript). Copy them into an online Python editor or your own computer.

How to learn effectively

  • Type the examples yourself instead of copy-pasting. Your fingers learn the syntax.
  • Change things and predict the output before running.
  • Read error messages from the bottom up: the last line says what went wrong; the lines above say where.
  • Build tiny projects as soon as possible: a tip calculator, a quiz, a file renamer.

Common mistakes

  • Inconsistent indentation (mixing tabs and spaces, or 2 and 4 spaces) → IndentationError.
  • Missing colon at the end of if, for, def lines → SyntaxError.
  • Capital letters: Print() is not print(). Python is case-sensitive.
  • Following Python 2 tutorials.

Exercise

  1. Open an online Python editor (or install Python in the next lesson) and print your name.
  2. Print the result of 365 * 24 (hours in a year).
  3. Print three words on one line using commas in print().
  4. Change the greeting program to greet four people, with a special message for names starting with "R".

Summary

  • Python is readable, beginner-friendly, and used for AI, data, automation and the web.
  • print() shows output; indentation (4 spaces) defines code blocks.
  • Learn Python 3 only.
  • Practise in an online editor or on your own computer.

Next, you'll install Python and set up an editor.

item.title: Installing Python
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
To write real programs, you'll want Python on your own computer. This lesson walks you through installing it on Windows, macOS and Linux, running code in two different ways, and setting up a good free editor.

Step 1: Download and install

Windows

  1. Go to python.org/downloads and click the big Download Python 3.x button.
  2. Run the installer.
  3. Important: tick "Add python.exe to PATH" at the bottom of the first screen. Without it, typing python in the terminal won't work.
  4. Click Install Now.

Python is also available in the Microsoft Store, which sets up the PATH automatically.

macOS

  1. Download the macOS installer from python.org/downloads and run it.
  2. Or, if you use Homebrew: brew install python.

macOS may include an older system Python used by the operating system. Always use the one you installed, with the command python3.

Linux

Most distributions already include Python 3. If not:

sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv   # Ubuntu / Debian
sudo dnf install python3                            # Fedora

Step 2: Check it works

Open a terminal (Windows: search for Terminal or Command Prompt; macOS: Terminal) and type:

python --version

On macOS and Linux, use python3:

python3 --version

You should see something like Python 3.13.1. Any version from 3.10 upward works for this course. If you see "command not found" or a Microsoft Store window on Windows, reinstall and make sure "Add to PATH" is ticked.

From here on, we'll write python; use python3 if that's what works on your computer.

Way 1: The interactive shell (REPL)

Type python alone and press Enter:

>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> "hello".upper()
'HELLO'
>>> name = "Asha"
>>> f"Hi {name}"
'Hi Asha'
>>> exit()

The >>> prompt means Python is waiting for a line. It runs each line immediately and shows the result. This is called a REPL (Read–Eval–Print Loop) and is perfect for quick experiments: "what does this function return?". Type exit() (or press Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux, Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows) to leave.

Way 2: Python files

Real programs live in files ending in .py. Create a folder, for example python-course, and a file inside it called hello.py:

name = input("What's your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
print("You just ran your first Python file.")

In the terminal, go to the folder and run it:

cd python-course
python hello.py

Type your name when asked. input() waits for the user to type something and press Enter.

Step 3: Set up an editor (VS Code)

You can write Python in any text editor, but a code editor helps a lot. Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is free and the most popular choice:

  1. Download it from code.visualstudio.com and install it.
  2. Open VS Code → Extensions (the squares icon on the left) → search Python → install the one by Microsoft.
  3. File → Open Folder → choose your python-course folder.
  4. Open hello.py and click the ▶ Run button in the top-right corner.

The output appears in the built-in terminal at the bottom. The Python extension also gives you:

  • Colour highlighting and error underlines as you type.
  • Autocomplete for functions and variables.
  • A debugger to run code step by step.

PyCharm Community (free) is another excellent Python-specific editor.

Step 4 (optional): Jupyter notebooks

Data scientists often use notebooks: documents that mix code, results, charts and notes. You can try them with no installation at colab.research.google.com (Google Colab), or in VS Code with the Jupyter extension. They're great for experiments; for programs and scripts, .py files are better.

Where pip fits in

Python comes with pip, a tool for installing extra packages (libraries others have written):

python -m pip --version

You'll use it in the "pip and Packages" lesson. For now, just check that this command prints a version.

Troubleshooting

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting "Add to PATH" on Windows.
  • Typing Python code into the terminal without starting python first (or the reverse: typing python hello.py inside the >>> shell).
  • **Saving files as hello.py.txt** with Notepad. Use a code editor.
  • Naming your file after a module, like random.py or math.py. It hides Python's own module of that name and causes confusing errors.

Exercise

  1. Install Python and check the version in the terminal.
  2. In the REPL, calculate 2 ** 100 (Python handles very big numbers).
  3. Create age.py that asks for the user's birth year with input() and prints their approximate age. (Hint: int(input(...)) converts the answer to a number; you'll learn why in lesson 5.)
  4. Install VS Code with the Python extension and run age.py from it.

Summary

  • Install Python 3 from python.org; on Windows, tick "Add python.exe to PATH".
  • Check with python --version (or python3).
  • The REPL (>>>) runs lines instantly; .py files hold real programs: python file.py.
  • VS Code with the Python extension is a great free editor.

Next, you'll learn the basic syntax rules of Python.

item.title: Python Syntax
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every language has grammar rules. Python's are few and simple, but strict: one wrong space or a missing colon stops the program. This lesson covers the rules you need for everything that follows.

Statements

A Python program is a list of statements, run from top to bottom. Normally, one statement per line:

price = 250
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print(total)

No semicolons are needed at the end of lines. (You *can* put two statements on one line with ;, but nobody does.)

Blocks and indentation

Statements that end with a colon : start a block: if, else, for, while, def, class, with, try. The block is everything indented beneath them:

temperature = 31

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot.")
    print("Stay hydrated.")
else:
    print("Nice weather.")

print("Done.")

Rules:

  • The line before a block ends with :.
  • Every line in the block is indented by the same amount, by convention 4 spaces.
  • The block ends when the indentation goes back.

Blocks can be nested:

score = 85
submitted = True

if submitted:
    if score >= 80:
        print("Excellent!")
    else:
        print("Submitted.")
else:
    print("Please submit your work.")

Indentation errors

if score > 50:
print("Pass")

This gives IndentationError: expected an indented block. Mixing tabs and spaces causes similar errors. Let your editor insert 4 spaces when you press Tab (VS Code does this by default for Python).

An empty block: pass

A block can't be empty. Use pass as a placeholder:

def coming_soon():
    pass  # TODO: write this later

coming_soon()
print("No error.")

Comments

# A full-line comment

total = 499 * 3  # a comment after code

# Python has no special multi-line comment.
# Just use several # lines.

Write comments that explain why, not what. # add 18% GST is useful; # multiply by 1.18 repeats the code.

Docstrings

A string right at the start of a function, class or file is a docstring, the documentation for it:

def area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

print(area(4, 5))
print(area.__doc__)

Editors show docstrings when you hover over the function. Triple quotes """ allow several lines.

Long lines

Keep lines under about 80–100 characters for readability. Inside brackets (), [] or {}, you can break lines freely:

total = (
    120 * 3
    + 250 * 1
    + 299 * 2
)

languages = [
    "HTML",
    "CSS",
    "JavaScript",
    "Python",
]

print(total, len(languages))

Names (identifiers)

Variable and function names:

  • Can contain letters, digits and underscores, but can't start with a digit.
  • Are case-sensitive: score, Score and SCORE are different.
  • Can't be keywords like if, for, def, class, True, None, import.

Python's naming style (from the official style guide, PEP 8):

Quotes

Strings can use single or double quotes; pick one style and be consistent:

a = 'single'
b = "double"
c = "It's easy"            # double quotes when the text has an apostrophe
d = """Several
lines of text"""
print(a, b, c)
print(d)

Reading error messages

Errors are normal. Python tells you exactly what happened in a traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shop.py", line 3, in <module>
    total = price * quantty
NameError: name 'quantty' is not defined. Did you mean: 'quantity'?

Read it from the bottom:

  1. The last line says the type of error and a message: a misspelled variable.
  2. The lines above show where: file shop.py, line 3, and the code on that line.

Modern Python even suggests fixes ("Did you mean…?"). Common error types:

The Zen of Python

Type this in the REPL:

import this

It prints 19 short principles behind Python's design, such as "Readability counts" and "Simple is better than complex". They're good advice for any code you write.

Common mistakes

  • Missing colon after if, for, def.
  • Mixing tabs and spaces.
  • Unclosed brackets or quotes: the error may point to the next line, so check the line above too.
  • Using a keyword as a name, like class = "A".

Exercise

  1. Write an if/else that checks whether a number is even, with two print lines inside the if block.
  2. Deliberately remove a colon and read the error. Then remove an indentation and read that error.
  3. Write a function with a docstring and print the docstring.
  4. Rename these to Python style: TotalPrice (a variable), getuser (a function), maxsize (a constant).

Summary

  • One statement per line; no semicolons.
  • A line ending in : starts a block; indent the block by 4 spaces.
  • # starts a comment; """docstrings""" document functions.
  • Use snake_case for names, and read tracebacks from the bottom.

Next, you'll store values in variables.

item.title: Python Variables
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A variable is a name that refers to a value, so you can use and change that value later. Python makes variables very simple: there's no special keyword, you just assign.

Creating variables

name = "Asha"
age = 21
height_m = 1.62
is_student = True

print(name, age, height_m, is_student)

= is the assignment operator: it stores the value on the right under the name on the left. A variable is created the first time you assign to it. No let, var or type declaration is needed.

Changing variables

score = 10
print(score)   # 10

score = 15
print(score)   # 15

score = score + 5
print(score)   # 20

score = score + 5 means: take the current value of score, add 5, store the result back in score.

Shortcut operators

points = 100
points += 20   # points = points + 20 → 120
points -= 5    # 115
points *= 2    # 230
points //= 3   # 76 (whole-number division)
print(points)

Python has no ++ or -- operators. Use count += 1.

Variables can change type

value = 42
print(type(value))   # <class 'int'>

value = "forty-two"
print(type(value))   # <class 'str'>

Python is dynamically typed: a variable can refer to any type of value, and type() tells you what it currently is. It's flexible, but changing a variable's type midway usually makes code confusing, so avoid it.

Names refer to objects

In Python, a variable is a label attached to a value (an object), not a box containing it. Two names can point to the same object:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # b refers to the SAME list
b.append(4)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]: a changed too!

For numbers and strings, this never surprises you, because they can't be changed in place (they're immutable). For lists and dictionaries (which are mutable), remember that assignment doesn't copy. Use b = a.copy() when you need an independent copy. You'll see this again in the Lists lesson.

Several assignments at once

x, y, z = 1, 2, 3
print(x, y, z)

first, last = "Meera Shah".split()
print(first)
print(last)

a = b = 0       # both names refer to 0
print(a, b)

The number of names must match the number of values, or you get a ValueError.

Swapping without a temporary variable

left = "tea"
right = "coffee"

left, right = right, left
print(left, right)   # coffee tea

Constants

Python has no true constants, but by convention names in UPPER_CASE shouldn't be changed:

GST_RATE = 0.18
MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 5

price = 1000
print(price * (1 + GST_RATE))

Putting such values in named constants at the top of a file makes the code self-explaining and easy to update.

Naming variables well

# Hard to understand
x = 1499
y = 3
z = x * y

# Clear
unit_price = 1499
quantity = 3
order_total = unit_price * quantity
print(order_total)

Rules and conventions:

  • Use snake_case: lower-case words joined with underscores.
  • Be descriptive: user_count, not uc.
  • Booleans read well as questions: is_active, has_paid.
  • Don't use names of built-in functions, like list, str, sum, max or input: you'd hide the real function.
sum = 10          # bad: hides the built-in sum()
# sum([1, 2, 3])  # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable
del sum           # removes our variable, restoring the built-in
print(sum([1, 2, 3]))

Printing variables with f-strings

The easiest way to combine text and variables is an f-string: put f before the quotes and variables inside { }:

name = "Rohan"
lessons_done = 7
total_lessons = 20

print(f"{name} has finished {lessons_done} of {total_lessons} lessons.")
print(f"Progress: {lessons_done / total_lessons:.0%}")
print(f"Next lesson: {lessons_done + 1}")

Output:

Rohan has finished 7 of 20 lessons.
Progress: 35%
Next lesson: 8
  • Any expression can go inside { }.
  • After a colon you can add a format: :.2f for 2 decimals, :.0% for a percentage, :, for thousands separators.
amount = 1234567.891
print(f"{amount:,.2f}")   # 1,234,567.89

A handy trick for debugging: print(f"{order_total=}") prints order_total=4497.

Deleting variables

del name removes a name. You'll rarely need it.

Common mistakes

  • Using a variable before assigning it → NameError.
  • Typos in names: totl instead of total creates a new variable or a NameError.
  • Shadowing built-ins like list, str or input.
  • **Forgetting the f** in f-strings, which prints the braces literally.
  • **Thinking b = a copies a list.**

Exercise

  1. Create variables for a product's name, price and quantity, and print a line like "3 × Notebook = ₹360" with an f-string.
  2. Start with balance = 1000, apply -= 250 and += 75, then print it.
  3. Swap two variables in one line.
  4. Create a constant DISCOUNT = 0.1 and print a price after the discount with 2 decimals.
  5. Show that b = a for a list doesn't copy it, then fix it with .copy().

Summary

  • name = value creates or updates a variable; no keyword or type is needed.
  • Names refer to objects; assigning a list to another name doesn't copy it.
  • Use snake_case names, UPPER_CASE for constants, and never shadow built-ins.
  • f-strings (f"{value}") are the easiest way to show variables in text.

Next, you'll learn Python's built-in data types.

item.title: Python Data Types
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every value in Python has a type that decides what you can do with it. You can add numbers, uppercase text, and append to lists, but not the other way round. This lesson is a tour of Python's built-in types; the following lessons explore each in depth.

Overview

count = 42                         # int: whole number
price = 19.99                      # float: decimal number
name = "Asha"                      # str: text
is_member = True                   # bool: True or False
nothing = None                     # NoneType: "no value"
scores = [92, 87, 95]              # list: ordered, changeable
point = (10, 20)                   # tuple: ordered, unchangeable
user = {"name": "Asha", "age": 21} # dict: key → value pairs
tags = {"python", "sql"}           # set: unique items, no order

for value in [count, price, name, is_member, nothing, scores, point, user, tags]:
    print(type(value).__name__, value)

Numbers: int and float

print(7 + 2, 7 - 2, 7 * 2)   # 9 5 14
print(7 / 2)                 # 3.5: / always gives a float
print(7 // 2)                # 3: whole-number (floor) division
print(7 % 2)                 # 1: remainder
print(2 ** 10)               # 1024: power
print(10 ** 30)              # ints can be as big as you like
  • int has no size limit.
  • float has about 15–17 significant digits, and some decimals can't be stored exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. The Numbers lesson covers how to handle this.

Strings: str

greeting = "Hello"
print(greeting + ", world")   # joining
print(greeting * 3)           # HelloHelloHello
print(len(greeting))          # 5
print(greeting[0])            # H

Strings are immutable: methods like .upper() return a new string. Full details in the Strings lesson.

Booleans: bool

is_open = True
is_raining = False
print(5 > 3)          # True
print(5 == 3)         # False
print(True + True)    # 2: True behaves like 1, False like 0

True and False start with capital letters.

None

None represents "no value" or "nothing yet":

winner = None

if winner is None:
    print("No winner yet.")

Compare with None using is (not ==). Functions that don't return anything return None.

Collections

Each gets its own lesson. Quick taste:

cart = ["pen", "notebook"]
cart.append("eraser")
print(cart)

prices = {"pen": 20, "notebook": 60}
print(prices["notebook"])

unique_cities = set(["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"])
print(unique_cities)  # {'Pune', 'Delhi'} (order may vary)

Checking types

print(type(3.0))                  # <class 'float'>
print(isinstance(3, int))         # True
print(isinstance("3", (int, float)))  # False: checks against several types

Prefer isinstance() in real code; it also handles subclasses.

Converting between types

print(int("42") + 8)        # 50
print(float("3.5") * 2)     # 7.0
print(str(99) + " points")  # "99 points"
print(int(7.9))             # 7: int() cuts off the decimals (doesn't round)
print(round(7.9))           # 8
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool("hi"))  # False False True
print(list("abc"))          # ['a', 'b', 'c']

Why conversion matters: input()

input() always returns a string, even if the user types a number:

# age = input("Your age: ")   # user types 20
age = "20"                    # what input() gives you
# print(age + 1)              # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
print(int(age) + 1)           # 21

Python never converts between text and numbers automatically. That's stricter than JavaScript, and it catches bugs early.

Converting invalid text raises an error:

try:
    int("twelve")
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

You'll learn try/except in the Errors and Exceptions lesson.

Truthy and falsy

In an if or while, every value counts as true or false. These are falsy:

falsy_values = [False, None, 0, 0.0, "", [], (), {}, set()]
for value in falsy_values:
    print(repr(value), bool(value))

Everything else is truthy, including "0", "False" and [0]. This allows short checks:

name = ""
if not name:
    print("Please enter your name.")

items = ["pen"]
if items:
    print(f"You have {len(items)} item(s).")

Mutable vs immutable

  • Immutable (can't change after creation): int, float, str, bool, None, tuple.
  • Mutable (can change): list, dict, set.

This matters when several names refer to the same object, and when using values as dictionary keys (keys must be immutable).

Common mistakes

  • Adding a string and a number: "Age: " + 21 → TypeError. Use an f-string or str().
  • **Forgetting that input() returns text.**
  • **Lower-case true / false / none** → NameError.
  • **Expecting int(7.9) to round.**
  • **Using == None** instead of is None.

Exercise

  1. Create one variable of each type in this lesson and print its type name.
  2. Ask (or pretend to ask) for two numbers as strings, convert them, and print their sum.
  3. Print 7 / 2, 7 // 2 and 7 % 2 and explain each result.
  4. Predict bool() of "0", 0, [], [0] and None, then check.
  5. Convert "3.99" to a float, multiply by 3, and print it rounded to 2 decimals.

Summary

  • Basic types: int, float, str, bool, None.
  • Collections: list, tuple, dict, set.
  • Check types with type() or isinstance(); convert with int(), float(), str(), bool(), list().
  • input() returns strings; Python never mixes text and numbers automatically.

Next, you'll work with text in depth: strings.
item.excerpt:encoded: Python's built-in types (int, float, str, bool, None, list, tuple, dict and set), checking types, converting between them, and truthy and falsy values.

item.title: Python Strings
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Strings hold text, and text is everywhere: names, messages, file contents, web pages, AI prompts. Python's strings come with dozens of built-in methods that make text processing short and readable.

Creating strings

single = 'Hello'
double = "It's Python"
multi = """Line one
Line two"""
escaped = "She said \"hi\"\nNew line\tTab"

print(single)
print(double)
print(multi)
print(escaped)

Escape sequences: \n (new line), \t (tab), \\ (backslash), \" and \' (quotes).

A raw string (prefix r) ignores escapes, which is handy for Windows paths and regular expressions:

print(r"C:\new\test")   # backslashes kept as they are

Indexing

word = "Python"
print(word[0])    # P: first character
print(word[5])    # n
print(word[-1])   # n: last character
print(word[-2])   # o
print(len(word))  # 6

Indexes start at 0. Negative indexes count from the end. word[6] would raise an IndexError.

Slicing

text[start:stop] takes characters from start up to, but not including, stop:

word = "Programming"
print(word[0:3])    # Pro
print(word[3:7])    # gram
print(word[:3])     # Pro: from the start
print(word[3:])     # gramming: to the end
print(word[-4:])    # ming: last 4
print(word[::2])    # Pormig: every second character
print(word[::-1])   # gnimmargorP: reversed

Slices never raise errors for out-of-range values; they just return what's available.

Strings are immutable

name = "asha"
# name[0] = "A"          # TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
name = name.capitalize() # create a new string and reassign
print(name)              # Asha

Every string method returns a new string. Remember to store the result.

Changing case

s = "learn PYTHON fast"
print(s.upper())       # LEARN PYTHON FAST
print(s.lower())       # learn python fast
print(s.title())       # Learn Python Fast
print(s.capitalize())  # Learn python fast
print(s.swapcase())    # LEARN python FAST

Cleaning: strip

raw = "   asha@example.com  \n"
print(repr(raw.strip()))     # 'asha@example.com'
print(repr(raw.lstrip()))    # only the left side
print("--hello--".strip("-"))  # hello

Always .strip() user input and lines read from files.

Searching

text = "Python is easy. Python is powerful."

print("easy" in text)             # True
print(text.startswith("Python"))  # True
print(text.endswith("."))         # True
print(text.find("is"))            # 7: first position, or -1 if not found
print(text.count("Python"))       # 2

in is the most Pythonic way to check if text contains something.

Replacing, splitting and joining

sentence = "I like cats. Cats are great."
print(sentence.replace("cats", "dogs"))   # replaces every "cats", but not "Cats": case-sensitive

csv_line = "Asha,21,Pune"
parts = csv_line.split(",")
print(parts)                 # ['Asha', '21', 'Pune']

words = "  many   spaces here ".split()  # no argument: split on any whitespace
print(words)                 # ['many', 'spaces', 'here']

print(" | ".join(["HTML", "CSS", "JS"]))  # HTML | CSS | JS
print("-".join("abc"))                    # a-b-c

split turns a string into a list; join (called on the separator) turns a list back into a string. Together they solve many text tasks.

Checking content

print("12345".isdigit())     # True
print("hello".isalpha())     # True
print("abc123".isalnum())    # True
print("   ".isspace())       # True
print("Hello".istitle())     # True

Useful for simple validation, e.g. checking a PIN code is all digits.

f-strings in depth

name = "Meera"
price = 1499.5
qty = 3
ratio = 0.4567

print(f"{name} bought {qty} items")
print(f"Total: ₹{price * qty:,.2f}")   # ₹4,498.50
print(f"Ratio: {ratio:.1%}")           # 45.7%
print(f"|{name:<10}|")                 # left-align in 10 characters
print(f"|{name:>10}|")                 # right-align
print(f"|{name:^10}|")                 # centre
print(f"{7:03d}")                      # 007: zero-padded
print(f"{name.upper()} has {len(name)} letters")

Format specs after the colon: , (thousands separator), .2f (2 decimals), % (percentage), < > ^ (alignment and width), 03d (zero-padding). Alignment is perfect for printing simple tables.

Looping over a string

word = "banana"
vowels = 0
for letter in word:
    if letter in "aeiou":
        vowels += 1
print(f"{word} has {vowels} vowels")

Comparing strings

print("apple" == "apple")        # True
print("Apple" == "apple")        # False: case matters
print("Apple".lower() == "apple".lower())  # True
print("apple" < "banana")        # True: alphabetical

For case-insensitive comparisons of international text, .casefold() is more thorough than .lower().

A practical example: make a URL slug

def slugify(title):
    cleaned = "".join(ch if ch.isalnum() or ch == " " else "" for ch in title)
    return "-".join(cleaned.lower().split())

print(slugify("  Python Strings: The Complete Basics! "))
# python-strings-the-complete-basics

The ch for ch in title part is a generator expression, a compact loop you'll understand better after the Lists and Loops lessons.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting strings are immutable: name.upper() alone does nothing visible; assign the result.
  • Off-by-one slices: s[0:3] gives 3 characters, indexes 0, 1, 2.
  • Case-sensitive comparisons and replacements.
  • Joining non-strings: ", ".join([1, 2]) fails; convert first: ", ".join(map(str, [1, 2])).

Exercise

  1. Take " hello WORLD " and turn it into "Hello world".
  2. Print the first 3 and last 3 characters of your full name.
  3. Check if a word is a palindrome using slicing (word == word[::-1]).
  4. Count how many times "the" appears in a sentence, ignoring case.
  5. Turn "red,green,blue" into "RED / GREEN / BLUE".
  6. Print a 3-row table of names and scores, aligned with f-string widths.

Summary

  • Index with s[i], slice with s[start:stop:step]; indexes start at 0, negatives count from the end.
  • Strings are immutable; methods return new strings.
  • Key methods: strip, lower/upper, replace, split, join, find, count, startswith.
  • f-strings with format specs handle numbers, percentages and alignment.

Next, you'll work with numbers and maths in Python.

item.title: Python Numbers
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Python is a favourite language for anything involving numbers, from shopping carts to scientific research. This lesson covers Python's number types, arithmetic, rounding, and the modules that handle maths, randomness and money.

int and float

students = 32          # int
average = 78.5         # float
big = 1_000_000        # underscores make big numbers readable
print(students, average, big)
print(type(students), type(average))
  • int: whole numbers of any size. 2 ** 200 works fine.
  • float: decimal numbers with about 15–17 digits of precision.
  • An operation with a float gives a float: 3 + 2.0 is 5.0.

Arithmetic operators

a, b = 17, 5
print(a + b)    # 22
print(a - b)    # 12
print(a * b)    # 85
print(a / b)    # 3.4: true division, always a float
print(a // b)   # 3: floor division
print(a % b)    # 2: remainder
print(a ** b)   # 1419857: power
print(-a // b)  # -4: floor division rounds DOWN, towards minus infinity

// and % are very useful together:

total_seconds = 3725
hours = total_seconds // 3600
minutes = (total_seconds % 3600) // 60
seconds = total_seconds % 60
print(f"{hours}h {minutes}m {seconds}s")   # 1h 2m 5s

print(divmod(17, 5))   # (3, 2): quotient and remainder in one step

Operator precedence follows maths rules: ** first, then * / // %, then + -. Use brackets when in doubt.

Float precision

print(0.1 + 0.2)              # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)       # False

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))  # True

Like in every language, binary floats can't store some decimals exactly. Compare floats with math.isclose(), round when displaying, and use Decimal for money (below).

Rounding

print(round(3.14159, 2))   # 3.14
print(round(7.5))          # 8
print(round(2.5))          # 2 (!)
print(round(3.5))          # 4

import math
print(math.floor(4.7))     # 4: always down
print(math.ceil(4.2))      # 5: always up
print(math.trunc(-4.7))    # -4: drop the decimals

round() uses banker's rounding: exact halves round to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2. This avoids bias in large statistics, but surprises people. For "school" rounding of money, use Decimal.

math.ceil is ideal for counting pages or boxes: 47 items at 10 per page need math.ceil(47 / 10) = 5 pages.

Useful built-in functions

numbers = [12, 7, 25, 3]
print(abs(-9))          # 9
print(min(numbers))     # 3
print(max(numbers))     # 25
print(sum(numbers))     # 47
print(sum(numbers) / len(numbers))  # 11.75: average
print(pow(2, 8))        # 256

The math module

import math

print(math.sqrt(144))         # 12.0
print(math.pi)                # 3.141592653589793
print(math.factorial(5))      # 120
print(math.gcd(24, 36))       # 12
print(math.log10(1000))       # 3.0
print(round(math.sin(math.pi / 2), 2))  # 1.0

radius = 7
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
print(f"Circle area: {area:.2f}")       # 153.94

import math loads the module; you'll learn more about modules in lesson 14.

Random numbers

import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))          # a dice roll: 1 to 6 inclusive
print(random.random())               # float from 0.0 up to 1.0
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))

cards = ["A", "K", "Q", "J"]
random.shuffle(cards)
print(cards)
print(random.sample(range(1, 50), 6))  # 6 unique lottery numbers

For passwords, tokens or anything security-related, use the secrets module instead: secrets.token_hex(16).

Exact decimals for money: Decimal

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

price = Decimal("19.99")
qty = 3
total = price * qty
print(total)                         # 59.97 exactly

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))   # 0.3 exactly

tax = (total * Decimal("0.18")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
print(tax)                           # 10.79
print(Decimal("2.5").quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))  # 3
  • Create Decimals from strings (Decimal("19.99")), not floats, or the float's imprecision comes along.
  • quantize rounds to a fixed number of places with the rounding rule you choose.

Banks, shops and accounting software use Decimal (or store amounts as whole paise/cents in ints).

Converting and validating numbers

print(int("42"), float("3.5"), int(3.99))   # 42 3.5 3
print(int("ff", 16))                        # 255: from hexadecimal
print(bin(10), hex(255))                    # 0b1010 0xff

text = "12a"
if text.isdigit():
    print(int(text))
else:
    print(f"'{text}' is not a whole number")

Formatting numbers

amount = 1234567.891
print(f"{amount:,.2f}")     # 1,234,567.89
print(f"{0.256:.1%}")       # 25.6%
print(f"{42:05d}")          # 00042
print(f"{1500000:.2e}")     # 1.50e+06

For Indian-style grouping (12,34,567) or currency symbols for any country, the third-party babel package handles locale-aware formatting.

Common mistakes

  • **Comparing floats with ==.** Use math.isclose.
  • **Expecting round(2.5) to be 3.**
  • Floats for money in serious applications. Use Decimal or integer paise.
  • **Decimal(0.1)** instead of Decimal("0.1").
  • Integer vs true division confusion: / always returns a float in Python 3.

Exercise

  1. Convert 500 minutes into hours and minutes using // and %.
  2. Calculate the area and circumference of a circle with radius 10, rounded to 2 decimals.
  3. Simulate rolling two dice 5 times and print each total.
  4. Calculate 3 items at ₹19.99 plus 18% tax using Decimal, rounded to 2 places.
  5. Find how many pages you need for 123 search results at 20 per page.

Summary

  • int for whole numbers, float for decimals; / gives floats, // floors, % gives remainders.
  • Floats can be imprecise: compare with math.isclose, use Decimal for money.
  • round() uses banker's rounding; math.floor/ceil always go down/up.
  • The math, random, decimal and secrets modules extend Python's number skills.

Next, you'll store collections of values in lists.

item.title: Python Lists
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A list is an ordered collection of items: a to-do list, a playlist, a set of exam scores. Lists are the most used data structure in Python, and they're very flexible: they can grow, shrink, be sorted and hold any kind of value.

Creating lists

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
scores = [92, 87, 95, 78]
mixed = ["Asha", 21, True, None]
empty = []
letters = list("abc")       # ['a', 'b', 'c']
numbers = list(range(1, 6)) # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

print(fruits, len(fruits))
print(numbers)

Indexing and slicing

Lists use the same indexing and slicing as strings:

colours = ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow", "purple"]
print(colours[0])     # red
print(colours[-1])    # purple
print(colours[1:3])   # ['green', 'blue']
print(colours[:2])    # ['red', 'green']
print(colours[::-1])  # reversed copy

Lists are mutable

Unlike strings, you can change a list in place:

tasks = ["wake up", "code", "sleep"]
tasks[1] = "code in Python"
print(tasks)

Adding items

cart = ["pen"]
cart.append("notebook")            # add one item to the end
cart.insert(0, "bag")              # insert at a position
cart.extend(["eraser", "ruler"])   # add several items
print(cart)   # ['bag', 'pen', 'notebook', 'eraser', 'ruler']

combined = [1, 2] + [3, 4]         # + makes a new list
print(combined)

append([1, 2]) would add the list as one item; extend adds each item separately.

Removing items

items = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "b"]

items.remove("b")      # removes the FIRST "b"
print(items)           # ['a', 'c', 'd', 'b']

last = items.pop()     # removes and returns the last item
print(last, items)     # b ['a', 'c', 'd']

first = items.pop(0)   # removes and returns item at index 0
print(first, items)    # a ['c', 'd']

del items[0]           # delete by index
print(items)           # ['d']

items.clear()          # remove everything
print(items)           # []

remove raises a ValueError if the item isn't there, so check with in first when unsure.

Searching

langs = ["python", "sql", "javascript", "sql"]
print("sql" in langs)        # True
print(langs.index("sql"))    # 1: first position
print(langs.count("sql"))    # 2

Sorting

nums = [42, 7, 19, 3]
nums.sort()                  # sorts the list in place
print(nums)                  # [3, 7, 19, 42]
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums)                  # [42, 19, 7, 3]

names = ["rohan", "Asha", "meera"]
print(sorted(names))                  # ['Asha', 'meera', 'rohan']: capitals first
print(sorted(names, key=str.lower))   # ['Asha', 'meera', 'rohan']: case-insensitive
print(sorted(names, key=len))         # ['Asha', 'rohan', 'meera']: by length
print(names)                          # unchanged: sorted() returns a new list
  • list.sort() changes the list and returns None.
  • sorted(list) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone.
  • key= sorts by a calculated value; very powerful with lists of dictionaries (lesson 10).

A common bug: nums = nums.sort() sets nums to None.

Looping over lists

scores = [72, 95, 88]

for score in scores:
    print(score)

for position, score in enumerate(scores, start=1):
    print(f"{position}. {score}")

names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name}: {score}")
  • enumerate gives you the position along with each item.
  • zip walks through several lists side by side.

Built-in functions with lists

scores = [72, 95, 88, 64]
print(len(scores), sum(scores), min(scores), max(scores))
print(f"Average: {sum(scores) / len(scores):.1f}")
print(any(s < 65 for s in scores))   # True: is any score below 65?
print(all(s >= 60 for s in scores))  # True: are all scores at least 60?

Copying lists

original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original           # NOT a copy: same list, two names
copy1 = original.copy()    # a real copy
copy2 = original[:]        # also a copy
copy3 = list(original)     # also a copy

original.append(4)
print(alias)   # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(copy1)   # [1, 2, 3]

These are shallow copies: if the list contains other lists, those inner lists are still shared. Use copy.deepcopy() for a full copy of nested data.

List comprehensions

A compact way to build a new list from another:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

squares = [n * n for n in numbers]
evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
labels = [f"Item {n}" for n in numbers[:3]]

print(squares)   # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36]
print(evens)     # [2, 4, 6]
print(labels)    # ['Item 1', 'Item 2', 'Item 3']

Read [n * n for n in numbers if n > 2] as "n squared, for each n in numbers, if n is greater than 2". The same with a loop:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
result = []
for n in numbers:
    if n > 2:
        result.append(n * n)
print(result)    # [9, 16, 25, 36]

Comprehensions are idiomatic Python. Keep them short; if one gets complicated, use a normal loop.

Nested lists

grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9],
]
print(grid[1][2])                     # 6: row 1, column 2
print([row[0] for row in grid])       # [1, 4, 7]: first column

Unpacking

first, second, *rest = ["gold", "silver", "bronze", "4th", "5th"]
print(first, second, rest)   # gold silver ['bronze', '4th', '5th']

Common mistakes

  • **nums = nums.sort()**, which sets nums to None.
  • **b = a thinking it copies.**
  • Changing a list while looping over it (removing items skips elements). Loop over a copy or build a new list with a comprehension.
  • **IndexError** from using an index equal to len(list).

Exercise

  1. Create a list of five cities. Add one, insert one at the start, and remove the third.
  2. Sort a list of numbers in descending order without changing the original.
  3. From [3, 8, 12, 5, 20, 7], make a list of only the numbers over 6, doubled, with a comprehension.
  4. Print a numbered shopping list with enumerate.
  5. Given two lists of names and ages, print "Name is Age" using zip.

Summary

  • Lists are ordered and mutable; index and slice them like strings.
  • append, insert, extend add; remove, pop, del, clear remove.
  • sort() changes the list; sorted() returns a new one; use key= for custom order.
  • Copy with .copy(); build lists concisely with comprehensions.

Next, you'll meet two more collections: tuples and sets.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create, index, slice and change lists; add, remove, sort and search items; copy lists safely; and write list comprehensions.

item.title: Python Tuples and Sets
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Lists are great general-purpose collections, but Python has two more that are better for specific jobs. Tuples hold a fixed group of values that shouldn't change. Sets hold unique items and answer "is this in here?" extremely fast.

Tuples

A tuple is like a list that can't be changed after it's created. It's written with round brackets:

point = (10, 20)
rgb = (37, 99, 235)
person = ("Asha", 21, "Pune")

print(point[0])      # 10
print(person[-1])    # Pune
print(len(rgb))      # 3
print(rgb[0:2])      # (37, 99)

Indexing, slicing, len, in, count and index all work just like with lists. What you can't do is change it:

point = (10, 20)
# point[0] = 15       # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
point = (15, 20)      # you can make a new tuple and reassign the name
print(point)

The comma makes the tuple

a = (5)      # just the number 5 in brackets
b = (5,)     # a tuple with one item
c = 5, 6     # brackets are optional
print(type(a), type(b), type(c))

Tuple unpacking

Tuples shine when you unpack them into variables:

person = ("Meera", 24, "Jaipur")
name, age, city = person
print(f"{name} ({age}) lives in {city}")

# Functions can return several values as a tuple
def min_max(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)

low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4])
print(low, high)   # 2 9

# Swapping uses tuple packing and unpacking
x, y = 1, 2
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)

When to use a tuple instead of a list

  • The data is a fixed record whose positions have meaning: coordinates (x, y), an RGB colour, a date (2024, 5, 1), a database row.
  • You want to protect the data from accidental changes.
  • You need it as a dictionary key or set item (lists can't be keys because they're mutable).
distances = {
    ("Pune", "Mumbai"): 150,
    ("Delhi", "Agra"): 233,
}
print(distances[("Pune", "Mumbai")])

A rule of thumb: lists for many items of the same kind; tuples for a few items of different kinds that belong together.

Named tuples

When positions get confusing, give them names:

from collections import namedtuple

Product = namedtuple("Product", ["name", "price", "stock"])
pen = Product("Pen set", 250, 30)
print(pen.name, pen.price)   # readable access by name
print(pen[1])                # still works by index

Sets

A set is an unordered collection of unique items, written with curly braces:

tags = {"python", "sql", "python", "html"}
print(tags)          # {'python', 'sql', 'html'}: duplicate removed, order not guaranteed
print(len(tags))     # 3

Removing duplicates

The most common use of sets:

cities = ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune", "Jaipur", "Delhi"]
unique = set(cities)
print(unique)              # 3 unique cities
print(sorted(unique))      # ['Delhi', 'Jaipur', 'Pune']: as a sorted list

# Keep the original order while removing duplicates:
print(list(dict.fromkeys(cities)))   # ['Pune', 'Delhi', 'Jaipur']

Fast membership tests

banned_words = {"spam", "scam", "free money"}
message = "this is not spam"

print("spam" in message.split())   # True
print("hello" in banned_words)     # False

Checking in on a list looks at every item one by one. A set uses hashing and finds the answer almost instantly, even with millions of items. If you check membership often, use a set.

Adding and removing

skills = {"html", "css"}
skills.add("javascript")
skills.update(["python", "sql"])
skills.discard("css")      # no error if missing
# skills.remove("java")    # KeyError if missing
print(skills)

Sets have no indexes (skills[0] is an error), because they have no order.

Empty set: {} creates an empty dictionary. Use set() for an empty set.

Set operations

python_devs = {"Asha", "Rohan", "Meera", "Kabir"}
sql_devs = {"Meera", "Kabir", "Sara"}

print(python_devs | sql_devs)   # union: knows either
print(python_devs & sql_devs)   # intersection: knows both → {'Meera', 'Kabir'}
print(python_devs - sql_devs)   # difference: Python but not SQL → {'Asha', 'Rohan'}
print(python_devs ^ sql_devs)   # symmetric difference: exactly one of them

print({"Meera"} <= sql_devs)    # subset check: True

The same operations exist as methods: union, intersection, difference, issubset.

A practical example

yesterday = {"asha@x.com", "rohan@x.com", "meera@x.com"}
today = {"rohan@x.com", "meera@x.com", "kabir@x.com"}

print("New subscribers:", today - yesterday)
print("Unsubscribed:", yesterday - today)
print("Stayed:", len(today & yesterday))

Comparing two lists of ids or emails is a one-liner with sets.

What can go in a set

Set items (and dictionary keys) must be hashable: immutable types like numbers, strings and tuples. Lists and dictionaries can't go in a set. frozenset is an immutable set, which can itself go in a set.

Choosing a collection

Common mistakes

  • **(5) instead of (5,)** for a one-item tuple.
  • **{} for an empty set** (it's a dict).
  • Expecting a set to keep order or support indexing.
  • Putting lists into sets → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

Exercise

  1. Create a tuple for a book (title, author, year) and unpack it into three variables.
  2. Write a function that returns the average and the highest of a list as a tuple, and unpack the result.
  3. Remove duplicates from [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 5] and print them sorted.
  4. Given two sets of students in two clubs, print who is in both, who is in only the first, and everyone.
  5. Check whether a username is in a set of 5 reserved names.

Summary

  • Tuples are ordered and immutable; great for fixed records, unpacking and dictionary keys.
  • Sets hold unique, unordered items; great for removing duplicates and fast in checks.
  • Set operations |, &, -, ^ compare collections in one line.
  • set() makes an empty set; {} makes an empty dict.

Next, you'll learn dictionaries: Python's key–value collection.
item.excerpt:encoded: Use tuples for fixed groups of values and unpacking, and sets for unique items, fast membership tests and set operations like union and intersection.

item.title: Python Dictionaries
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A dictionary (dict) stores data as key–value pairs: a word and its meaning, a product and its price, a setting and its value. You look values up by key instead of by position. Dictionaries are everywhere in Python, and they map directly to JSON, the data format of the web.

Creating dictionaries

user = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 21,
    "city": "Pune",
    "skills": ["Python", "SQL"],
}

prices = {"pen": 20, "notebook": 60, "bag": 899}
empty = {}
from_pairs = dict(name="Rohan", age=25)

print(user)
print(len(prices))     # 3

Keys are usually strings, but can be any immutable value (numbers, tuples). Values can be anything, including lists and other dictionaries. Since Python 3.7, dictionaries keep the order in which keys were added.

Reading values

user = {"name": "Asha", "age": 21}

print(user["name"])                 # Asha
# print(user["email"])              # KeyError: 'email'

print(user.get("email"))            # None: no error
print(user.get("email", "not set")) # not set: default value
print("age" in user)                # True: checks keys

Use dict[key] when the key must exist (a missing key is a bug), and .get(key, default) when it might be missing.

Adding, changing and deleting

stock = {"pen": 40, "notebook": 12}

stock["eraser"] = 25          # add a new key
stock["pen"] = 35             # change an existing value
stock["notebook"] += 10       # update based on the old value

del stock["eraser"]           # delete a key (KeyError if missing)
removed = stock.pop("pen")    # delete and return the value
print(removed, stock)         # 35 {'notebook': 22}

stock.update({"ruler": 15, "notebook": 30})  # add/overwrite several keys
print(stock)

Looping over dictionaries

scores = {"Asha": 92, "Rohan": 78, "Meera": 85}

for name in scores:                  # loops over keys
    print(name)

for score in scores.values():
    print(score)

for name, score in scores.items():   # keys and values together
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

print(list(scores.keys()))

.items() is the most common way to loop over a dictionary.

Sorting by value

scores = {"Asha": 92, "Rohan": 78, "Meera": 85}

ranking = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
for position, (name, score) in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
    print(f"{position}. {name} – {score}")

print(max(scores, key=scores.get))   # Asha: key with the highest value

lambda item: item[1] is a tiny inline function that returns the value of each (key, value) pair; you'll learn lambdas in the Functions lesson.

Nested data

Real data is often dictionaries inside lists inside dictionaries, exactly like JSON from an API:

order = {
    "id": 1042,
    "customer": {"name": "Rohan", "city": "Delhi"},
    "items": [
        {"product": "Notebook", "price": 120, "qty": 3},
        {"product": "Pen set", "price": 250, "qty": 1},
    ],
    "paid": True,
}

print(order["customer"]["city"])          # Delhi
print(order["items"][0]["product"])       # Notebook

total = sum(item["price"] * item["qty"] for item in order["items"])
print(f"Order {order['id']} total: ₹{total}")   # ₹610

Notice order['id'] with single quotes inside the double-quoted f-string.

A list of dictionaries

The most common shape for tabular data:

students = [
    {"name": "Asha", "score": 92, "city": "Pune"},
    {"name": "Rohan", "score": 78, "city": "Delhi"},
    {"name": "Meera", "score": 85, "city": "Pune"},
]

top = [s["name"] for s in students if s["score"] >= 80]
print(top)                                         # ['Asha', 'Meera']

by_score = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)
print([s["name"] for s in by_score])               # ['Asha', 'Meera', 'Rohan']

average = sum(s["score"] for s in students) / len(students)
print(f"Average: {average:.1f}")                   # 85.0

Counting and grouping

Counting how often things appear is a classic dictionary task:

words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split()

counts = {}
for word in words:
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
print(counts)   # {'the': 3, 'cat': 1, 'and': 2, 'dog': 1, 'bird': 1}

from collections import Counter
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))   # [('the', 3), ('and', 2)]

Grouping items by a key:

students = [
    {"name": "Asha", "city": "Pune"},
    {"name": "Rohan", "city": "Delhi"},
    {"name": "Meera", "city": "Pune"},
]

by_city = {}
for s in students:
    by_city.setdefault(s["city"], []).append(s["name"])
print(by_city)   # {'Pune': ['Asha', 'Meera'], 'Delhi': ['Rohan']}

setdefault(key, default) returns the value for the key, first inserting the default if the key is missing. (collections.defaultdict(list) does the same job.)

Dictionary comprehensions

prices = {"pen": 20, "notebook": 60, "bag": 899}

with_tax = {item: round(price * 1.18, 2) for item, price in prices.items()}
cheap = {item: price for item, price in prices.items() if price < 100}
squares = {n: n * n for n in range(1, 6)}

print(with_tax)
print(cheap)     # {'pen': 20, 'notebook': 60}
print(squares)   # {1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16, 5: 25}

Merging and copying

defaults = {"theme": "light", "font_size": 16}
user_settings = {"theme": "dark"}

settings = defaults | user_settings      # Python 3.9+: later values win
print(settings)                          # {'theme': 'dark', 'font_size': 16}

copy = settings.copy()                   # shallow copy
copy["theme"] = "blue"
print(settings["theme"])                 # still dark

Common mistakes

  • **KeyError** from d[key] on a missing key; use .get() or check with in.
  • Looping and changing size: adding or deleting keys while looping over a dict raises an error. Loop over list(d) instead.
  • Using mutable values as keys (lists) → TypeError.
  • **Expecting in to check values**: "Asha" in scores.values() checks values; plain in checks keys.

Exercise

  1. Create a dictionary of five countries and their capitals. Print each as "Capital of X is Y".
  2. Write a word-frequency counter for a sentence of your choice, ignoring case.
  3. Given a list of product dicts with name, category and price, group the names by category.
  4. Find the most expensive product with max(..., key=...).
  5. Make a dict comprehension that maps each word in a list to its length.

Summary

  • Dictionaries map keys to values; read with d[key] or safely with d.get(key, default).
  • Add or change with d[key] = value; remove with del or pop.
  • Loop with .items(); sort with sorted(d.items(), key=...).
  • Lists of dicts model tables and JSON; Counter, setdefault and comprehensions make counting and grouping easy.

Next, you'll make decisions with if, elif and else.

item.title: Python If/Else
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Programs become useful when they can decide: approve or reject, show a warning or not, charge shipping or give it free. Python's if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true.

if

temperature = 34

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot today.")
    print("Remember to drink water.")

print("Have a nice day.")

The condition is followed by a colon, and the block is indented. If the condition is false, the indented lines are skipped.

else and elif

age = 16

if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")
else:
    print(f"You can vote in {18 - age} years.")

For more than two options, use elif ("else if"):

score = 76

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 75:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 40:
    grade = "D"
else:
    grade = "F"

print(f"Score {score}: grade {grade}")   # Score 76: grade B

Python checks each condition from the top and runs only the first block whose condition is true. That's why the order matters: 95 is also >= 75, but it's caught by the first condition.

Comparison operators

Python lets you chain comparisons, just like in maths:

age = 25
if 18 <= age < 60:
    print("Working age")

and, or, not

age = 22
has_ticket = True
is_vip = False

if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Welcome to the concert.")

if is_vip or age < 12:
    print("Free entry.")
else:
    print("Standard entry.")

if not has_ticket:
    print("Please buy a ticket.")

Python uses the words and, or and not instead of symbols. and is evaluated before or; use brackets to make mixed conditions clear.

Truthy checks

Empty strings, empty collections, 0 and None count as false:

username = "   ".strip()
cart = []

if not username:
    print("Please enter a username.")

if cart:
    print(f"{len(cart)} items in cart")
else:
    print("Your cart is empty.")

This is the Pythonic way: write if cart: rather than if len(cart) > 0:.

Membership: in

day = "sat"
if day in ("sat", "sun"):
    print("Weekend!")

email = "asha@example.com"
if "@" not in email:
    print("Invalid email")
else:
    print("Looks like an email")

in works with strings, lists, tuples, sets and dictionary keys, and replaces long chains of or.

Identity: is

Use is to compare with None (and True/False in rare cases):

result = None
if result is None:
    print("No result yet.")

== asks "are these equal?"; is asks "is this the very same object?". For None, always use is.

Nested conditions and guard clauses

Nested ifs work but get hard to read:

def can_checkout(user, cart):
    if user is not None:
        if cart:
            if user.get("address"):
                return "OK"
            else:
                return "Add an address"
        else:
            return "Cart is empty"
    else:
        return "Please log in"

print(can_checkout({"address": "Pune"}, ["book"]))

The same logic with guard clauses (return early on problems):

def can_checkout(user, cart):
    if user is None:
        return "Please log in"
    if not cart:
        return "Cart is empty"
    if not user.get("address"):
        return "Add an address"
    return "OK"

print(can_checkout({"address": "Pune"}, []))
print(can_checkout(None, ["book"]))

Flat code is easier to read and extend. (You'll learn def and return in the Functions lesson.)

Conditional expressions (one-line if)

age = 20
status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"
print(status)

items = 3
print(f"{items} item{'s' if items != 1 else ''}")

value_if_true if condition else value_if_false: handy for choosing between two values. Use a full if statement for anything longer.

match: choosing from many patterns (Python 3.10+)

command = "stop"

match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting…")
    case "stop" | "quit":
        print("Stopping.")
    case "help":
        print("Commands: start, stop, help")
    case _:
        print(f"Unknown command: {command}")
  • case "stop" | "quit" matches either value.
  • case _ matches anything else (like else).
  • No break needed; only one case runs.

match can also unpack structures:

point = (0, 5)

match point:
    case (0, 0):
        print("Origin")
    case (0, y):
        print(f"On the y-axis at {y}")
    case (x, 0):
        print(f"On the x-axis at {x}")
    case (x, y):
        print(f"At {x}, {y}")

For simple value checks, if/elif is often clearer; match shines with many fixed options or structured data.

A practical example: shipping cost

def shipping_cost(total, is_member, city):
    if is_member:
        return 0
    if total >= 500:
        return 0
    if city in {"Pune", "Mumbai"}:
        return 30
    return 60

print(shipping_cost(350, False, "Pune"))    # 30
print(shipping_cost(350, False, "Delhi"))   # 60
print(shipping_cost(800, False, "Delhi"))   # 0
print(shipping_cost(100, True, "Delhi"))    # 0

Common mistakes

  • **= instead of ==** in a condition: if x = 5: is a SyntaxError in Python (good, it catches the bug).
  • Missing colon or wrong indentation.
  • Wrong order of elif branches.
  • **if x == "a" or "b":** is always true; write if x in ("a", "b"):.
  • **== None** instead of is None.

Exercise

  1. Ask for a number (or set one) and print whether it's positive, negative or zero.
  2. Write a BMI category checker: under 18.5, 18.5–24.9, 25–29.9, 30 and above.
  3. Given an hour (0–23), print "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening".
  4. Check if a year is a leap year: divisible by 4, except centuries, unless divisible by 400.
  5. Write a match statement for a simple calculator that handles +, -, * and /.

Summary

  • if, elif and else run different blocks based on conditions; the first true branch wins.
  • Combine conditions with and, or and not; chain comparisons like 0 < x < 10.
  • Use in for membership, is None for None, and truthy checks for empty values.
  • Conditional expressions and match handle short choices and many fixed options.

Next, you'll repeat actions with for and while loops.
