item.title: Python Loops
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Loops let a program repeat work: process every line in a file, every product in a list, or keep asking until the user types a valid answer. Python has two loops: for (go through a collection) and while (repeat while a condition is true).

for loops

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]

for fruit in fruits:
    print(f"I like {fruit}")

for item in collection: takes each item in turn. It works with lists, tuples, strings, sets, dictionaries, files and more.

for letter in "Hi!":
    print(letter)

prices = {"pen": 20, "bag": 899}
for item, price in prices.items():
    print(f"{item}: ₹{price}")

range(): counting

for i in range(5):
    print(i)           # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)           # 1 to 5

for i in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(i)           # 10, 8, 6, 4, 2

range(start, stop, step) produces numbers from start up to, but not including, stop. With one argument it starts at 0.

n = 7
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(f"{n} × {i} = {n * i}")

enumerate and zip

tasks = ["Write code", "Test", "Deploy"]
for number, task in enumerate(tasks, start=1):
    print(f"{number}. {task}")

names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]
scores = [92, 78, 85]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name} scored {score}")

Avoid writing for i in range(len(tasks)): and then tasks[i]. enumerate and zip are clearer and less error-prone.

Accumulating results

Many loops build up a result:

cart = [("Notebook", 120, 3), ("Pen set", 250, 1), ("USB cable", 299, 2)]

total = 0
expensive = []
for name, price, qty in cart:
    total += price * qty
    if price > 200:
        expensive.append(name)

print(f"Total: ₹{total}")              # ₹1208
print("Items over ₹200:", expensive)

while loops

while repeats as long as its condition is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many rounds you need:

balance = 1000
years = 0

while balance < 2000:
    balance *= 1.08          # 8% interest per year
    years += 1

print(f"Doubled after {years} years: ₹{balance:,.2f}")

Make sure something in the loop changes the condition, or it will run forever. If a program gets stuck, press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop it.

Input validation with while

answers = iter(["abc", "-5", "42"])   # pretend the user types these in turn

while True:
    text = next(answers)              # in a real program: text = input("Enter a positive number: ")
    if text.isdigit() and int(text) > 0:
        number = int(text)
        break
    print(f"'{text}' is not a positive number, try again.")

print(f"Thanks! You entered {number}.")

while True with a break is a common pattern for "keep asking until the answer is valid". (iter and next here just simulate typing so the example runs on its own.)

break and continue

numbers = [4, 9, -1, 16, 25]

for n in numbers:
    if n < 0:
        print("Found a negative number, stopping.")
        break
    print(n ** 0.5)

for n in range(1, 11):
    if n % 3 == 0:
        continue        # skip multiples of 3
    print(n, end=" ")
print()
  • break leaves the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this round and starts the next one.

print(..., end=" ") prints a space instead of a new line at the end.

Loop else

A for or while loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without break:

users = ["asha", "rohan", "meera"]
search = "kabir"

for user in users:
    if user == search:
        print("Found!")
        break
else:
    print(f"{search} not found.")

It's perfect for search loops: "if we never found it, do this".

Nested loops

for row in range(1, 4):
    for col in range(1, 4):
        print(row * col, end="\t")
    print()

Output:

1	2	3
2	4	6
3	6	9

The inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer loop.

Loops vs comprehensions

When a loop just builds a list, a comprehension is shorter:

prices = [120, 250, 299, 1499]

# loop
with_tax = []
for p in prices:
    with_tax.append(round(p * 1.18))

# comprehension: same result
with_tax = [round(p * 1.18) for p in prices]
print(with_tax)

And built-in functions often replace loops entirely: sum(), min(), max(), any(), all(), sorted().

Don't change a list while looping over it

numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
for n in numbers:
    if n == 2:
        numbers.remove(n)
print(numbers)   # [1, 2, 3, 4]: one 2 was skipped!

numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
numbers = [n for n in numbers if n != 2]
print(numbers)   # [1, 3, 4]: correct

Removing items shifts the rest, so the loop skips one. Build a new list instead.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one with range: range(1, 10) stops at 9.
  • Infinite while loops that never update their condition.
  • **for i in range(len(x))** when you only need the items.
  • Modifying a list while iterating it.
  • Indentation: a line accidentally inside (or outside) the loop.

Exercise

  1. Print the numbers 1–20, but "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, and "FizzBuzz" for both.
  2. Sum all even numbers from 1 to 100 with a loop, then with sum(range(...)).
  3. Count the vowels in a sentence.
  4. Use a while loop to find how many years it takes ₹10,000 to reach ₹20,000 at 7% per year.
  5. Search a list of names with a for ... else loop and print a message if the name isn't found.

Summary

  • for item in collection loops over items; range() produces numbers to count with.
  • enumerate adds positions; zip walks several collections together.
  • while repeats while a condition is true; break exits, continue skips ahead.
  • A loop's else runs when no break happened; prefer comprehensions and built-ins for simple loops.

Next, you'll organise code into reusable functions.
item.excerpt:encoded: Repeat code with for and while loops, use range, enumerate and zip, control loops with break, continue and else, and avoid common loop bugs.

item.title: Python Functions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A function is a named, reusable block of code. Functions let you write logic once and use it everywhere, give meaningful names to steps, and test pieces of a program separately. Every good Python program is built from small functions.

Defining and calling a function

def greet():
    print("Hello! Welcome to VitalStack.")

greet()
greet()
  • def starts the definition, followed by the name, brackets and a colon.
  • The indented block is the function's body.
  • greet() calls (runs) it. Defining a function doesn't run it.

Parameters and arguments

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Rohan")

name is a parameter (a placeholder); "Asha" is an argument (the actual value).

Returning values

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 4)
print(result)               # 7
print(add(add(1, 2), 10))   # 13

return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. A function without return returns None.

def describe_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        return "invalid"
    if age < 18:
        return "minor"
    return "adult"

print(describe_age(25), describe_age(12), describe_age(-1))

print vs return

def double_print(n):
    print(n * 2)       # shows it, returns None

def double_return(n):
    return n * 2       # gives it back

a = double_print(5)    # prints 10
b = double_return(5)   # prints nothing
print(a, b)            # None 10

Return values so other code can use them; print only when the job is to show something.

Returning several values

def stats(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers), sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

low, high, average = stats([72, 95, 88, 64])
print(low, high, round(average, 1))   # 64 95 79.8

Python returns a tuple, which you can unpack.

Default values

def make_tea(sugar=1, milk=True):
    return f"Tea with {sugar} sugar(s){' and milk' if milk else ''}"

print(make_tea())
print(make_tea(2))
print(make_tea(0, milk=False))

Parameters with defaults must come after those without.

Never use a mutable default like [] or {}:

def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []          # a fresh list every call
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item("pen"))       # ['pen']
print(add_item("book"))      # ['book'], not ['pen', 'book']

A default [] is created once and shared by every call, a famous Python gotcha. Use None and create the list inside.

Keyword arguments

You can pass arguments by name, in any order:

def create_user(name, role="student", active=True):
    return {"name": name, "role": role, "active": active}

print(create_user("Asha", active=False))
print(create_user(role="teacher", name="Rohan"))

Keyword arguments make calls self-explaining: send_email(to=..., subject=..., urgent=True) is clearer than send_email(..., ..., True).

*args and **kwargs

def total(*prices):
    return sum(prices)

print(total(10, 20, 30))      # 60

def describe(**details):
    for key, value in details.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")

describe(name="Meera", city="Jaipur", age=24)
  • *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
  • **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

You can also unpack into a call:

def area(width, height):
    return width * height

size = (4, 5)
print(area(*size))                     # 20
print(area(**{"width": 2, "height": 3}))  # 6

Docstrings and type hints

def price_with_tax(price: float, rate: float = 0.18) -> float:
    """Return the price including tax, rounded to 2 decimals.

    rate is a fraction: 0.18 means 18%.
    """
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

print(price_with_tax(1000))
help(price_with_tax)
  • The docstring documents what the function does; help() and editors show it.
  • Type hints (price: float, -> float) document the expected types. Python doesn't enforce them, but editors and tools like mypy use them to catch mistakes. They're very common in modern code.

Scope

Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only during the call.

def calculate():
    result = 6 * 7
    return result

print(calculate())
# print(result)   # NameError: result only existed inside the function

Functions can read variables from outside, but to reassign one you'd need the global keyword, which is usually a sign of bad design. Pass values in as parameters and return results instead.

TAX = 0.18                  # a module-level constant: fine to read

def with_tax(price):
    return price * (1 + TAX)

print(with_tax(100))

Functions are objects

You can store functions in variables, put them in lists and pass them to other functions:

def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

def whisper(text):
    return text.lower() + "…"

for style in (shout, whisper):
    print(style("Hello"))

words = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))   # pass a function as the key

Lambda: tiny anonymous functions

square = lambda n: n * n
print(square(6))   # 36

students = [("Asha", 92), ("Rohan", 78), ("Meera", 85)]
print(sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True))

lambda params: expression creates a one-line function without a name. Use lambdas for short key= functions; use def for anything longer.

Writing good functions

  • One job per function, with a name that says what it does: calculate_total, is_valid_email.
  • Short: if it doesn't fit on your screen, split it.
  • Input through parameters, output through return, no hidden global changes.
  • Docstring for anything non-obvious.
def is_valid_email(email: str) -> bool:
    """Very basic email check: one @ and a dot after it."""
    if email.count("@") != 1:
        return False
    local, domain = email.split("@")
    return bool(local) and "." in domain

print(is_valid_email("asha@example.com"))  # True
print(is_valid_email("asha@example"))      # False

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to call the function (greet instead of greet()).
  • **Forgetting return**, then getting None.
  • Mutable default arguments.
  • Too many positional parameters; use keyword arguments for clarity.
  • Relying on global variables instead of parameters.

Exercise

  1. Write celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) and test it with 0, 37 and 100.
  2. Write is_even(n) returning True or False, and use it with a list comprehension to filter evens.
  3. Write average(*numbers) that returns 0 for no numbers instead of crashing.
  4. Write format_price(amount, currency="₹", decimals=2) returning a string like "₹1,499.00".
  5. Sort a list of (product, price) tuples by price with a lambda.

Summary

  • def name(params): defines a function; name(args) calls it; return gives back a value.
  • Defaults, keyword arguments, *args and **kwargs make functions flexible; avoid mutable defaults.
  • Docstrings and type hints document functions.
  • Local variables live only inside the call; functions are objects you can pass around; lambdas are one-line functions.

Next, you'll split code into modules and use Python's standard library.
item.excerpt:encoded: Define functions with def, use parameters, return values, default and keyword arguments, *args and **kwargs, type hints, docstrings, scope and lambda.

item.title: Python Modules
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
As programs grow, one long file becomes hard to manage. Modules let you split code into files and reuse it. Python also ships with a huge standard library of ready-made modules: "batteries included". Knowing what's in it saves you from reinventing the wheel.

What is a module?

Any .py file is a module. Python's own modules work the same way: math, random, datetime are just Python (or compiled) files installed with Python.

Importing

import math

print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi)

import math loads the module once, and you use its contents with math.name. The prefix makes it clear where each name comes from.

Other ways to import

from math import sqrt, pi          # import specific names
print(sqrt(16), pi)

import datetime as dt              # import with a shorter alias
print(dt.date.today().year >= 2024)

from random import choice as pick  # alias a single name
print(pick(["a", "b", "c"]))

Avoid from module import *: it dumps every name into your file, making it unclear where things come from and risking name clashes.

Some aliases are universal conventions: import numpy as np, import pandas as pd.

A tour of the standard library

datetime: dates and times

from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

today = date(2024, 5, 1)
deadline = today + timedelta(days=14)
print(deadline)                              # 2024-05-15
print((deadline - today).days)               # 14
print(deadline.strftime("%d %b %Y"))         # 15 May 2024

moment = datetime.fromisoformat("2024-05-01T14:30:00")
print(moment.hour, moment.strftime("%I:%M %p"))   # 14 02:30 PM

random, math and statistics

import statistics

marks = [72, 95, 88, 64, 88]
print(statistics.mean(marks))     # 81.4
print(statistics.median(marks))   # 88
print(statistics.mode(marks))     # 88

os and pathlib: files and folders

from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("reports")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "summary.txt").write_text("All good.")

for path in folder.iterdir():
    print(path.name, path.suffix, path.stat().st_size, "bytes")

pathlib makes paths work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. / joins path parts.

json: reading and writing JSON

import json

data = {"name": "Asha", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"], "active": True}
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(text)
print(json.loads(text)["skills"][0])   # Python

More in the "Working with JSON and APIs" lesson.

collections: smarter containers

from collections import Counter, defaultdict

print(Counter("mississippi").most_common(2))   # [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]

groups = defaultdict(list)
for name, city in [("Asha", "Pune"), ("Rohan", "Delhi"), ("Kabir", "Pune")]:
    groups[city].append(name)
print(dict(groups))

Other useful modules

The official documentation at docs.python.org lists them all.

Writing your own module

Create two files in the same folder.

pricing.py:

"""Helpers for prices and tax."""

GST_RATE = 0.18

def with_tax(price, rate=GST_RATE):
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

def format_inr(amount):
    return f"₹{amount:,.2f}"

shop.py:

import pricing

price = pricing.with_tax(1499)
print(pricing.format_inr(price))      # ₹1,768.82

Run python shop.py. Python finds pricing.py because it's in the same folder as the script you ran. Now any other script can reuse your pricing logic.

if __name__ == "__main__"

When Python runs a file directly, it sets the special variable __name__ to "__main__". When the file is imported, __name__ is the module's name instead. This lets a file be both a reusable module and a runnable script:

def with_tax(price, rate=0.18):
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

def main():
    print("Quick check:", with_tax(100))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()   # runs only when you execute this file directly, not on import

Use this pattern in every script: it keeps test code and command-line behaviour from running when someone imports your functions.

Packages: folders of modules

A package is a folder of modules, usually with an __init__.py file:

my_app/
├── main.py
└── utils/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── pricing.py
    └── dates.py

Import with dots:

from utils.pricing import with_tax
from utils import dates

Large projects (Django, pandas) are organised as packages of packages.

How Python finds modules

When you import x, Python searches, in order:

  1. The folder of the script you ran.
  2. The standard library.
  3. Installed third-party packages (from pip, next-but-one lesson).

That's why you must never name your file after a module you use: a file called random.py or json.py in your folder hides the real module, and import random loads yours instead, with confusing errors like "module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'".

Exploring a module

import math
print(dir(math)[:10])      # names inside the module
help(math.ceil)            # documentation for one function

In VS Code, hover over a name or Ctrl+click it to jump to its source.

Common mistakes

  • Naming your files math.py, random.py, email.py, json.py…
  • **from module import *.**
  • Circular imports: a.py imports b.py which imports a.py. Move shared code into a third module.
  • **Forgetting if __name__ == "__main__":**, so importing a file runs its script code.

Exercise

  1. Use datetime to print how many days are left until 31 December of this year.
  2. Use statistics to find the mean and median of 10 numbers.
  3. Create a module textutils.py with word_count(text) and reverse_words(text), and use it from another file.
  4. Add a main() function with the __name__ check to your module and test both running and importing it.
  5. Use Counter to find the three most common words in a paragraph.

Summary

  • Every .py file is a module; import reuses its code.
  • from x import y and import x as alias control naming; avoid import *.
  • The standard library covers dates, files, JSON, maths, randomness and much more.
  • Use if __name__ == "__main__": for script code, and organise big projects into packages.

Next, you'll read and write files.

item.title: Python Files
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Programs often need to keep data after they stop: logs, settings, reports, exported spreadsheets. Python makes reading and writing files simple. In this lesson you'll work with text files and CSV files, the format every spreadsheet program understands.

Writing a file

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("First line\n")
    f.write("Second line\n")

print("Saved.")
  • open(filename, mode) opens a file and returns a file object.
  • Mode "w" means write: it creates the file, or erases it if it already exists.
  • \n adds a line break; write doesn't add one for you.
  • encoding="utf-8" makes sure all characters (₹, é, Hindi, emoji) are saved correctly on every operating system.

Why with?

with automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error happens. An unclosed file may not have all its data saved, and the operating system can run out of file handles. Always use with for files.

Reading a file

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("First line\nSecond line\nThird line\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    content = f.read()           # the whole file as one string

print(content)

Mode "r" (read) is the default.

Line by line

For big files, read one line at a time instead of loading everything into memory:

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("apple\nbanana\n\ncherry\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        line = line.strip()          # remove the \n at the end
        if not line:
            continue                 # skip empty lines
        print(number, line)

Each line includes its \n, so .strip() it. You can also get a list of lines with f.read().splitlines().

Appending

Mode "a" adds to the end of the file without erasing it. Perfect for logs:

from datetime import datetime

def log(message):
    with open("app.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(f"{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S} {message}\n")

log("App started")
log("User signed in")

with open("app.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

File modes

Be careful with "w": opening an existing file in write mode deletes its contents immediately.

Handling missing files

try:
    with open("does_not_exist.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        print(f.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found. Check the name and folder.")

You'll learn try/except fully in the next lesson.

pathlib: the modern way to handle paths

from pathlib import Path

reports = Path("reports")
reports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)               # create the folder if needed

file = reports / "summary.txt"             # join paths with /
file.write_text("Sales: ₹12,400\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

print(file.exists(), file.name, file.stem, file.suffix)
print(file.resolve())                       # the full absolute path

for txt in reports.glob("*.txt"):           # find files by pattern
    print("Found:", txt)

Path works on Windows, macOS and Linux without worrying about \ vs /. For small files, read_text and write_text are a one-line alternative to open.

Where is the file?

Relative paths like "notes.txt" are relative to the current working directory: the folder you ran Python from, which isn't always where the script lives. To use files next to your script:

from pathlib import Path
HERE = Path(__file__).parent
data_file = HERE / "data.txt"

CSV files

CSV (comma-separated values) is the simplest spreadsheet format. Excel and Google Sheets can open and save it. Use the csv module rather than splitting on commas yourself, because values can contain commas inside quotes.

Writing CSV

import csv

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "price": 120, "stock": 50},
    {"name": "Pen set", "price": 250, "stock": 30},
    {"name": "Backpack, large", "price": 1899, "stock": 12},
]

with open("products.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "price", "stock"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(products)

print(open("products.csv", encoding="utf-8").read())

Note newline="", which the csv module needs to avoid blank lines on Windows. "Backpack, large" is automatically quoted because it contains a comma.

Reading CSV

import csv

with open("products.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("name,price,stock\nNotebook,120,50\nPen set,250,30\n\"Backpack, large\",1899,12\n")

with open("products.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    total_value = 0
    for row in reader:
        value = int(row["price"]) * int(row["stock"])
        total_value += value
        print(f"{row['name']:<16} ₹{value:>7,}")

print(f"Inventory value: ₹{total_value:,}")

DictReader gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header row. All values are strings, so convert numbers with int() or float().

Reading files in other encodings

If you get a UnicodeDecodeError, the file was saved with a different encoding. Files from older Windows programs are often "cp1252"; Excel's "CSV UTF-8" format uses "utf-8-sig". Try open(name, encoding="utf-8-sig").

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting with**, leaving files open.
  • **Using "w" when you meant "a"**, erasing data.
  • **Forgetting \n** when writing lines.
  • Not stripping lines when reading, leaving \n in your data.
  • Treating CSV values as numbers without converting.
  • Wrong working directory, so the file "isn't found" even though it exists.

Exercise

  1. Write a program that saves five of your favourite films to films.txt, one per line, then reads them back with numbers.
  2. Add a "journal" function that appends today's date and a message to journal.txt.
  3. Count the lines, words and characters in a text file.
  4. Write a CSV of three students with name and score, then read it and print the average score.
  5. Use pathlib to list every .txt file in a folder with its size.

Summary

  • with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f: opens files safely; they close automatically.
  • "r" reads, "w" overwrites, "a" appends; loop over a file to read line by line.
  • pathlib.Path builds paths and reads/writes small files easily.
  • The csv module (DictReader, DictWriter) handles spreadsheets correctly; convert values from strings.

Next, you'll handle errors gracefully with try and except.

item.title: Python Errors and Exceptions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Things go wrong: users type letters where numbers belong, files go missing, networks drop. When Python hits a problem it can't handle, it raises an exception and stops the program. With try and except, you can catch exceptions and respond sensibly instead of crashing.

Syntax errors vs exceptions

  • A syntax error means the code isn't valid Python (missing colon, unclosed bracket). The program doesn't start at all. You fix these by correcting the code.
  • An exception happens while the program runs: the code is valid, but something fails at that moment.
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
# print(numbers[10])   # IndexError: list index out of range
# int("abc")           # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
# 10 / 0               # ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# {"a": 1}["b"]        # KeyError: 'b'
# "age" + 5            # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
print("Each commented line above would raise a different exception.")

try and except

text = "abc"

try:
    number = int(text)
    print(f"You entered {number}")
except ValueError:
    print(f"'{text}' is not a whole number.")

print("The program keeps running.")
  • Code that might fail goes in try.
  • If an exception of the named type happens, Python jumps to the matching except block.
  • If nothing fails, the except block is skipped.

Catch specific exceptions

def safe_divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Can't divide by zero.")
        return None
    except TypeError:
        print("Both values must be numbers.")
        return None

print(safe_divide(10, 2))
print(safe_divide(10, 0))
print(safe_divide(10, "2"))

Several except blocks handle different problems differently. You can also catch several types in one block: except (ValueError, TypeError):.

Don't catch everything blindly

# Avoid:
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except:                # catches EVERYTHING, even Ctrl+C and typos in your own code
    print("Something went wrong")

A bare except: (or except Exception: used carelessly) hides real bugs: a misspelled variable becomes "something went wrong" with no clue why. Catch the specific exceptions you expect and know how to handle.

Getting the error message

try:
    value = int("12.5")
except ValueError as error:
    print("Problem:", error)
    print("Type:", type(error).__name__)

as error gives you the exception object, whose text explains the problem. It's useful for logging.

else and finally

def read_number(text):
    try:
        number = float(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"Invalid: {text!r}")
    else:
        print(f"Valid number: {number}")     # runs only if no exception
    finally:
        print("Check complete.")             # always runs

read_number("3.14")
read_number("pi")
  • else runs only when the try block succeeded. Keep the try block small and put the follow-up code in else, so you don't accidentally catch errors from it.
  • finally always runs, error or not. It's for clean-up: closing connections, deleting temporary files, stopping a timer. (with blocks do this automatically for files.)

A real pattern: retrying user input

attempts = iter(["twelve", "-3", "12"])   # simulated user input

while True:
    raw = next(attempts)                   # in a real program: raw = input("Quantity: ")
    try:
        quantity = int(raw)
        if quantity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("must be positive")
    except ValueError as error:
        print(f"'{raw}' isn't valid ({error}). Try again.")
    else:
        break

print(f"Ordering {quantity} items.")

Raising exceptions

Your own functions should raise exceptions when they receive bad input, rather than returning wrong results silently:

def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Amount must be positive.")
    if amount > balance:
        raise ValueError(f"Insufficient funds: balance is {balance}.")
    return balance - amount

print(withdraw(1000, 300))

try:
    withdraw(1000, 5000)
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

raise ExceptionType("message") stops the function and passes the problem to the caller, who decides what to do (show a message, retry, log it). This separates detecting a problem from handling it.

Custom exceptions

For bigger programs, define your own exception types so callers can catch exactly your errors:

class InsufficientFundsError(Exception):
    """Raised when a withdrawal is larger than the balance."""

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise InsufficientFundsError(f"Need {amount}, have {self.balance}")
        self.balance -= amount

account = Account(500)
try:
    account.withdraw(800)
except InsufficientFundsError as error:
    print("Declined:", error)

You'll learn classes properly in the next lesson; a custom exception just needs class Name(Exception):.

EAFP: Python's style

Python code often follows "Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission": try the operation and handle the exception, instead of checking everything first.

settings = {"theme": "dark"}

# Look before you leap (LBYL)
if "font_size" in settings:
    size = settings["font_size"]
else:
    size = 16

# EAFP
try:
    size = settings["font_size"]
except KeyError:
    size = 16

print(size)

Both are fine; here settings.get("font_size", 16) is shortest of all. EAFP is especially useful for files and networks, where the situation can change between checking and acting.

Reading tracebacks

When an exception isn't caught, Python prints a traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shop.py", line 12, in <module>
    total = checkout(cart)
  File "shop.py", line 7, in checkout
    return sum(item["price"] for item in cart)
  File "shop.py", line 7, in <genexpr>
    return sum(item["price"] for item in cart)
KeyError: 'price'

Read it bottom-up: the last line is the error (KeyError: 'price', an item without a price). Above it is the chain of calls, ending with the exact line that failed. Look at the deepest line in your code first.

Common exception types

Common mistakes

  • **Bare except:** that hides bugs.
  • **Huge try blocks** that catch errors from unrelated lines.
  • Silently ignoring errors (except: pass), so problems go unnoticed.
  • Returning error codes like -1 instead of raising exceptions.

Exercise

  1. Write to_int(text) that returns an int, or None with a printed message if conversion fails.
  2. Write get_item(items, index) that returns the item or "not found" using try/except IndexError.
  3. Read a file name from a variable and print its contents, with a friendly message if it doesn't exist.
  4. Write set_age(age) that raises ValueError for ages below 0 or above 130, and call it inside try.
  5. Create a custom OutOfStockError and raise it from a buy(product, qty) function.

Summary

  • Exceptions are runtime errors; try/except catches them so your program can respond.
  • Catch specific exception types; use as error to read the message.
  • else runs on success; finally always runs for clean-up.
  • raise signals problems in your own functions; custom exceptions make errors precise.

Next, you'll model real-world things with classes and objects.
item.excerpt:encoded: Handle errors with try, except, else and finally, catch specific exceptions, raise your own, create custom exception classes, and read tracebacks.

item.title: Python Classes and Objects
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
So far you've used Python's built-in types: strings, lists, dictionaries. Classes let you create your own types that bundle data and behaviour together: a BankAccount with a balance and a deposit() method, a Product with a price and a discounted() method. This style is called object-oriented programming (OOP).

Class and object

  • A class is a blueprint: it describes what data and abilities something has.
  • An object (or instance) is one thing built from that blueprint.

You've already used objects: "hello" is an object of class str, and .upper() is one of its methods.

Defining a class

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
bella = Dog("Bella", 5)

print(rex.name, rex.age)    # Rex 3
print(bella.bark())         # Bella says woof!
  • class Dog: defines the class. Class names use PascalCase.
  • __init__ is the initialiser: it runs automatically when you create an object and sets up its data.
  • self is the object being created or used. self.name = name stores the value on that object.
  • bark is a method: a function that belongs to the class. Its first parameter is always self.
  • Dog("Rex", 3) creates an object; Python passes the new object as self automatically.

Each object has its own data: changing rex.age doesn't affect bella.

A more useful example: a bank account

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance
        self.history = []

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive.")
        self.balance += amount
        self.history.append(("deposit", amount))

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount
        self.history.append(("withdraw", amount))

account = BankAccount("Asha", 1000)
account.deposit(500)
account.withdraw(200)
print(account.balance)      # 1300
print(account.history)      # [('deposit', 500), ('withdraw', 200)]

The object keeps its own state (balance, history), and the methods are the only intended way to change it, with rules built in. That's the main benefit of classes: data and the rules for changing it live together.

Class attributes

Attributes defined directly in the class are shared by all objects:

class Product:
    tax_rate = 0.18             # class attribute: same for every product

    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name        # instance attributes: different per product
        self.price = price

    def price_with_tax(self):
        return round(self.price * (1 + Product.tax_rate), 2)

pen = Product("Pen set", 250)
bag = Product("Backpack", 1899)
print(pen.price_with_tax(), bag.price_with_tax())   # 295.0 2240.82

Use class attributes for constants and settings shared by all instances. Don't use a mutable class attribute (like a list) for per-object data: every object would share the same list.

Special methods: __str__ and __repr__

Printing an object normally shows something unhelpful like <__main__.Product object at 0x7f…>. Special methods (with double underscores, "dunder" methods) customise built-in behaviour:

class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name} (₹{self.price:,})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Product({self.name!r}, {self.price})"

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Product) and (self.name, self.price) == (other.name, other.price)

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.price < other.price

items = [Product("Backpack", 1899), Product("Notebook", 120), Product("Pen set", 250)]
print(items[0])                     # Backpack (₹1,899)
print(items)                        # uses __repr__ for items inside a list
print(sorted(items))                # sorting works thanks to __lt__
print(Product("A", 1) == Product("A", 1))   # True thanks to __eq__
  • __str__: friendly text for print() and str().
  • __repr__: unambiguous text for developers, shown in lists and the REPL.
  • __eq__, __lt__: make == and sorting work.
  • Others include __len__ (for len()), __add__ (for +) and __contains__ (for in).

Properties: computed and protected attributes

class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):
        return self.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

    @property
    def celsius(self):
        return self._celsius

    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError("Below absolute zero!")
        self._celsius = value

t = Temperature(25)
print(t.fahrenheit)     # 77.0: computed, used like an attribute
t.celsius = 30          # goes through the setter's check
print(t.fahrenheit)     # 86.0

@property turns a method into something you read like an attribute. A setter adds validation. A leading underscore (_celsius) is a convention meaning "internal: don't touch from outside". Python doesn't enforce privacy; it trusts developers to respect the convention.

Inheritance

A class can inherit from another, reusing its code and adding or changing behaviour:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: ₹{self.balance:,}"

class SavingsAccount(Account):
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=0.04):
        super().__init__(owner, balance)     # run the parent's __init__
        self.rate = rate

    def add_interest(self):
        self.balance += round(self.balance * self.rate)

    def describe(self):                       # override the parent method
        return super().describe() + f" (savings, {self.rate:.0%})"

s = SavingsAccount("Meera", 10000)
s.add_interest()
s.withdraw(400)                               # inherited method
print(s.describe())                           # Meera: ₹10,000 (savings, 4%)
print(isinstance(s, Account))                 # True
  • class SavingsAccount(Account): inherits everything from Account.
  • super() calls the parent's version of a method.
  • Defining a method with the same name overrides the parent's.

Use inheritance for genuine "is a" relationships (a savings account is an account). For "has a" relationships (a car has an engine), store one object inside another instead; this is called composition and is often simpler.

Dataclasses: less boilerplate

For classes that mainly hold data, dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Expense:
    title: str
    amount: float
    category: str = "other"
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def is_large(self):
        return self.amount > 1000

e = Expense("Groceries", 1450.5, "food")
print(e)                 # Expense(title='Groceries', amount=1450.5, category='food', tags=[])
print(e.is_large())      # True
print(e == Expense("Groceries", 1450.5, "food"))   # True

field(default_factory=list) gives each object its own new list (the safe way to have a mutable default). Dataclasses are used a lot in modern Python, and you'll use one in the project lesson.

When to use classes

Use a class when you have data and behaviour that belong together, or you need many objects of the same kind with their own state. For a simple calculation, a function is enough; for simple records, a dictionary or dataclass often is.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting self** as the first method parameter, or forgetting self. when using attributes (balance += 1 instead of self.balance += 1).
  • Calling the method on the class instead of an object: Dog.bark().
  • Mutable class attributes shared by accident.
  • Deep inheritance trees; prefer composition and keep hierarchies shallow.

Exercise

  1. Create a Book class with title, author and pages, and a __str__ like "Title by Author (300 pages)".
  2. Add a method is_long() that returns True for books over 400 pages.
  3. Create a Rectangle class with area and perimeter properties.
  4. Create a Student class with a list of marks and methods add_mark(mark) and average().
  5. Create Shape with area() returning 0, and Circle and Square subclasses that override it. Put several shapes in a list and print their areas.

Summary

  • A class is a blueprint; objects are instances with their own data.
  • __init__ sets up attributes on self; methods are functions that take self.
  • Special methods like __str__, __eq__ and __lt__ hook into Python's built-in behaviour.
  • Properties compute or validate attributes; inheritance reuses and extends classes; dataclasses remove boilerplate.

Next, you'll install third-party packages with pip and manage them with virtual environments.

item.title: Python pip and Packages
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Python's standard library is big, but the real superpower is the ecosystem: over half a million free packages on PyPI (the Python Package Index) for web apps, data analysis, AI, automation and more. pip is the tool that installs them. In this lesson you'll install packages the professional way, inside virtual environments.

What is a package?

A package is code someone else wrote and published so you can use it with import. Examples:

Step 1: Create a virtual environment

If you install every package into your main Python, different projects soon need different versions of the same package and break each other. A virtual environment (venv) is a private folder of packages for one project.

In your project folder:

python -m venv .venv

This creates a .venv folder containing a copy of Python and an empty set of packages. (Use python3 on macOS and Linux.)

Step 2: Activate it

# Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). While it's active, python and pip refer to the environment's versions, and packages install into .venv only. Type deactivate to leave.

VS Code detects .venv automatically and offers to use it; if not, press Ctrl+Shift+P → Python: Select Interpreter and choose the .venv one.

(On Windows PowerShell, if activation is blocked, run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once.)

Step 3: Install packages

pip install requests

pip downloads requests and everything it depends on from PyPI. Then use it in your code:

import requests

response = requests.get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1", timeout=10)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.json()["title"])

Useful pip commands

pip install requests pandas      # install several
pip install "requests==2.32.3"   # an exact version
pip install --upgrade requests   # upgrade to the latest
pip uninstall requests           # remove
pip list                         # what's installed in this environment
pip show requests                # details: version, dependencies, location

If pip isn't found, use python -m pip install …, which always uses the pip belonging to the Python you're running.

Step 4: Record your dependencies

So others (or you, on another computer or a server) can recreate the environment:

pip freeze > requirements.txt

requirements.txt lists every installed package with its exact version:

certifi==2024.8.30
charset-normalizer==3.4.0
idna==3.10
requests==2.32.3
urllib3==2.2.3

To install everything from it in a fresh environment:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # or the Windows command
pip install -r requirements.txt

This is the standard way to share Python projects. Commit requirements.txt to Git, but not the .venv folder: add .venv/ to your .gitignore.

Modern projects often use a pyproject.toml file and tools like uv or Poetry, which do the same job faster with more features. The ideas (an isolated environment plus a list of dependencies) are the same.

Choosing packages safely

Anyone can publish to PyPI, so choose carefully:

  • Check the name exactly. Attackers publish look-alike packages ("requets", "python-dateutils") hoping for typos. This is called typosquatting.
  • Look at the project page on pypi.org: recent releases, a link to source code, documentation, and how widely it's used.
  • Prefer well-known packages for common tasks.
  • Pin versions in requirements.txt, so an update can't suddenly change behaviour.
  • **Never run sudo pip install** on Linux/macOS; it can break the system Python. Use a venv.

Example: a tiny weather-style script with requests

import requests

def get_user(user_id):
    url = f"https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/{user_id}"
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
        response.raise_for_status()      # raises an error for 4xx/5xx responses
    except requests.RequestException as error:
        print("Request failed:", error)
        return None
    return response.json()

user = get_user(1)
if user:
    print(f"{user['name']} works at {user['company']['name']}")

You'll go deeper into APIs and JSON in the next lesson.

Example: a quick chart with matplotlib

pip install matplotlib
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")               # draw to a file, no window needed
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"]
sales = [12000, 15500, 14200, 18900]

plt.bar(months, sales, color="#2563eb")
plt.title("Monthly sales (₹)")
plt.savefig("sales.png", dpi=120)
print("Saved sales.png")

A few lines to a chart image. This is why Python is so popular for data work.

Common mistakes

  • Installing without activating the venv, so packages land in the wrong Python.
  • **ModuleNotFoundError** because VS Code uses a different interpreter than the one where you installed the package.
  • **Committing .venv** to Git (it's large and machine-specific).
  • Typos in package names.
  • **Naming your own file requests.py**, which hides the real package.

Exercise

  1. Create a folder api-practice, make a virtual environment and activate it.
  2. Install requests and print the titles of the first 5 posts from https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts.
  3. Run pip freeze > requirements.txt and look at the file.
  4. Delete .venv, recreate it, and reinstall from requirements.txt.
  5. Install matplotlib and make a line chart of your weekly study hours.

Summary

  • PyPI hosts hundreds of thousands of packages; pip install name installs them.
  • Use a virtual environment per project: python -m venv .venv, then activate it.
  • pip freeze > requirements.txt records versions; pip install -r requirements.txt restores them.
  • Check package names and sources carefully, and never install with sudo.

Next, you'll work with JSON data and web APIs.
item.excerpt:encoded: Install third-party packages from PyPI with pip, isolate projects with virtual environments, record dependencies in requirements.txt, and choose packages safely.

item.title: Python JSON and APIs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most data on the internet travels as JSON, and most online services (weather, payments, maps, AI models) are used through APIs. Python is excellent at both. In this lesson you'll convert data to and from JSON, save it in files, and talk to real web APIs.

JSON and Python

JSON looks almost exactly like Python dictionaries and lists:

{
  "name": "Asha",
  "age": 21,
  "skills": ["Python", "SQL"],
  "active": true,
  "manager": null
}

Python → JSON text: dumps

import json

user = {"name": "Asha", "age": 21, "skills": ["Python", "SQL"], "active": True, "manager": None}

text = json.dumps(user)
print(text)
print(type(text))          # str

pretty = json.dumps(user, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
print(pretty)
  • json.dumps ("dump string") converts Python data to a JSON string.
  • indent=2 makes it readable.
  • ensure_ascii=False keeps characters like ₹ or Hindi readable instead of ₹ escapes.

Not everything can be converted: sets, dates and custom objects raise a TypeError. Convert them first (list(my_set), my_date.isoformat()).

JSON text → Python: loads

import json

text = '{"product": "Notebook", "price": 120, "tags": ["paper", "school"]}'
data = json.loads(text)

print(data["product"], data["price"] * 2)
print(data["tags"][0])

Invalid JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError; catch it when the text comes from outside your program.

Saving and loading JSON files

import json

settings = {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 18, "recent": ["lesson-1", "lesson-2"]}

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=2)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded == settings)   # True
print(loaded["recent"])

dump/load (without the "s") work directly with files. JSON files are a simple, human-readable way to store settings and small amounts of data, and you'll use them in the project lesson.

What is an API?

A web API is a set of URLs that return data for programs. You send an HTTP request; the server sends back a response with a status code and usually a JSON body.

We'll practise with JSONPlaceholder (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com), a free fake API for learning.

Calling an API with the standard library

No installation needed:

import json
from urllib.request import urlopen

with urlopen("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1", timeout=10) as response:
    user = json.load(response)

print(user["name"])
print(user["address"]["city"])

This works, but error handling and sending data are clumsy with urllib. Most developers use the requests package instead.

Calling an API with requests

Install it inside your virtual environment first: pip install requests.

import requests

response = requests.get(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts",
    params={"userId": 1},
    timeout=10,
)

print(response.status_code)          # 200
posts = response.json()              # parse the JSON body
print(len(posts), "posts")
for post in posts[:3]:
    print("-", post["title"])
  • params= builds the query string (?userId=1) for you.
  • timeout= stops your program waiting forever if the server doesn't answer. Always set it.
  • response.json() parses the body into Python data.

Handling errors properly

import requests

def fetch_user(user_id):
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            f"https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/{user_id}", timeout=10
        )
        response.raise_for_status()           # error for 4xx and 5xx
        return response.json()
    except requests.Timeout:
        print("The server took too long.")
    except requests.HTTPError as error:
        print(f"HTTP error: {error.response.status_code}")
    except requests.RequestException as error:
        print("Network problem:", error)
    return None

print(fetch_user(2)["name"])
print(fetch_user(9999))                      # 404 → prints an error, returns None

Networks fail. A robust program expects that and responds gracefully.

Sending data: POST

import requests

new_post = {"title": "Learning APIs", "body": "Python makes this easy.", "userId": 1}

response = requests.post(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts",
    json=new_post,          # converts to JSON and sets the Content-Type header
    timeout=10,
)

print(response.status_code)   # 201
print(response.json())        # the server's copy, with a new id

json= does the conversion for you. Other methods: requests.put, requests.patch, requests.delete.

API keys and secrets

Real APIs (weather, maps, payments, AI) usually need a key to identify you, sent in a header:

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("WEATHER_API_KEY")
if not api_key:
    print("Set the WEATHER_API_KEY environment variable first.")
else:
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}
    # response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather", headers=headers,
    #                         params={"city": "Pune"}, timeout=10)

Never write keys directly in your code, especially code you put on GitHub. Bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Keep them in environment variables (or a .env file listed in .gitignore, loaded with the python-dotenv package).

Being a good API citizen

  • Read the API's documentation and rate limits. Getting a 429 means slow down; time.sleep() between requests helps.
  • Cache results you reuse instead of requesting them again.
  • Respect the terms of use, especially for scraping or storing data.

A complete small example

import json
import requests

def top_todos(user_id, limit=5):
    response = requests.get(
        "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos",
        params={"userId": user_id},
        timeout=10,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    todos = response.json()
    done = sum(1 for t in todos if t["completed"])
    summary = {
        "user_id": user_id,
        "total": len(todos),
        "completed": done,
        "open_titles": [t["title"] for t in todos if not t["completed"]][:limit],
    }
    with open(f"user_{user_id}_summary.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(summary, f, indent=2)
    return summary

print(json.dumps(top_todos(1), indent=2))

Fetch → process → save as JSON: the shape of countless real automation scripts.

Common mistakes

  • **Confusing dumps/loads (strings) with dump/load (files).**
  • Single quotes in JSON: {'a': 1} is valid Python but invalid JSON.
  • No timeout, so the program hangs.
  • Not checking the status code before using response.json().
  • API keys in source code.

Exercise

  1. Save a dictionary of your favourite books to books.json and load it back.
  2. Fetch https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users and print each user's name and email.
  3. Count how many todos are completed for user 3.
  4. Send a POST request creating a new todo and print the response.
  5. Handle the error when requesting /users/9999.

Summary

  • json.dumps/loads convert between Python and JSON text; dump/load work with files.
  • APIs return JSON over HTTP; check status codes and always set timeouts.
  • requests makes GET and POST calls easy; raise_for_status() turns HTTP errors into exceptions.
  • Keep API keys in environment variables, never in code.

item.title: Python Project: Simple Expense Tracker
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Time to put the whole Python course into one useful program: a command-line expense tracker. You'll be able to add expenses, list them, see totals by category and month, delete mistakes, and export everything to a CSV file you can open in Excel. The data is saved to a JSON file, so it's still there next time.

What you'll build

=== Expense Tracker ===
1. Add expense
2. List expenses
3. Summary by category
4. Monthly totals
5. Delete expense
6. Export to CSV
0. Quit
Choose an option:

Create a folder expense-tracker with one file, tracker.py. We'll build it in steps; the complete program is at the end.

Step 1: The data model

Each expense has an id, a date, a description, a category and an amount. A dataclass is perfect:

from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import date

@dataclass
class Expense:
    id: int
    day: str            # ISO date, e.g. "2024-05-01"
    description: str
    category: str
    amount: float

e = Expense(1, date(2024, 5, 1).isoformat(), "Lunch", "food", 180.0)
print(e)
print(asdict(e))        # a plain dict, ready to save as JSON

Storing dates as ISO strings ("2024-05-01") keeps them JSON-friendly and sortable.

Step 2: Saving and loading

import json
from pathlib import Path

DATA_FILE = Path("expenses.json")

def load_expenses():
    if not DATA_FILE.exists():
        return []
    try:
        with DATA_FILE.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return [Expense(**item) for item in json.load(f)]
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError) as error:
        print(f"Could not read {DATA_FILE}: {error}. Starting with an empty list.")
        return []

def save_expenses(expenses):
    with DATA_FILE.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump([asdict(e) for e in expenses], f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

Expense(**item) unpacks each saved dictionary into the dataclass. If the file is damaged, we warn and continue rather than crash.

Step 3: Getting valid input

Users make typos. Helper functions keep asking until the input is valid:

from datetime import date

def ask_amount(prompt):
    while True:
        text = input(prompt).strip().replace(",", "")
        try:
            amount = float(text)
            if amount <= 0:
                raise ValueError
            return round(amount, 2)
        except ValueError:
            print("Please enter a positive number, e.g. 249.50")

def ask_date(prompt):
    while True:
        text = input(prompt).strip()
        if not text:
            return date.today().isoformat()       # Enter = today
        try:
            return date.fromisoformat(text).isoformat()
        except ValueError:
            print("Use the format YYYY-MM-DD, or press Enter for today.")

Step 4: Adding and listing

CATEGORIES = ["food", "transport", "bills", "shopping", "health", "other"]

def next_id(expenses):
    return max((e.id for e in expenses), default=0) + 1

def add_expense(expenses):
    description = input("Description: ").strip() or "(no description)"
    print("Categories:", ", ".join(CATEGORIES))
    category = input("Category: ").strip().lower()
    if category not in CATEGORIES:
        print("Unknown category, using 'other'.")
        category = "other"
    amount = ask_amount("Amount (₹): ")
    day = ask_date("Date (YYYY-MM-DD, Enter for today): ")
    expense = Expense(next_id(expenses), day, description, category, amount)
    expenses.append(expense)
    save_expenses(expenses)
    print(f"Added #{expense.id}: {description} – ₹{amount:,.2f}")

def list_expenses(expenses):
    if not expenses:
        print("No expenses yet.")
        return
    print(f"{'ID':>3}  {'Date':<10}  {'Category':<10}  {'Amount':>10}  Description")
    for e in sorted(expenses, key=lambda e: (e.day, e.id)):
        print(f"{e.id:>3}  {e.day:<10}  {e.category:<10}  {e.amount:>10,.2f}  {e.description}")
    print(f"{'Total':>27}  {sum(e.amount for e in expenses):>10,.2f}")

f-string widths (:>3, :<10, :>10,.2f) line the columns up like a table.

Step 5: Reports

from collections import defaultdict

def summary_by_category(expenses):
    totals = defaultdict(float)
    for e in expenses:
        totals[e.category] += e.amount
    grand_total = sum(totals.values())
    if not grand_total:
        print("No expenses yet.")
        return
    for category, total in sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True):
        share = total / grand_total
        bar = "█" * round(share * 30)
        print(f"{category:<10} ₹{total:>10,.2f}  {share:>4.0%}  {bar}")

def monthly_totals(expenses):
    months = defaultdict(float)
    for e in expenses:
        months[e.day[:7]] += e.amount          # "2024-05-01"[:7] → "2024-05"
    for month in sorted(months):
        print(f"{month}  ₹{months[month]:>10,.2f}")

The category report even draws a little bar chart with text characters.

Step 6: Deleting and exporting

import csv

def delete_expense(expenses):
    try:
        expense_id = int(input("ID to delete: "))
    except ValueError:
        print("Please enter a number.")
        return
    for e in expenses:
        if e.id == expense_id:
            confirm = input(f"Delete '{e.description}' (₹{e.amount:,.2f})? [y/N] ")
            if confirm.lower() == "y":
                expenses.remove(e)
                save_expenses(expenses)
                print("Deleted.")
            return
    print(f"No expense with id {expense_id}.")

def export_csv(expenses, path="expenses.csv"):
    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["id", "day", "description", "category", "amount"])
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(asdict(e) for e in expenses)
    print(f"Exported {len(expenses)} expenses to {path}")

utf-8-sig makes Excel display the ₹ sign and other special characters correctly.

Step 7: The menu

def main():
    expenses = load_expenses()
    actions = {
        "1": add_expense,
        "2": list_expenses,
        "3": summary_by_category,
        "4": monthly_totals,
        "5": delete_expense,
        "6": export_csv,
    }
    while True:
        print("\n=== Expense Tracker ===")
        print("1. Add expense\n2. List expenses\n3. Summary by category")
        print("4. Monthly totals\n5. Delete expense\n6. Export to CSV\n0. Quit")
        choice = input("Choose an option: ").strip()
        if choice == "0":
            print("Goodbye!")
            break
        action = actions.get(choice)
        if action:
            action(expenses)
        else:
            print("Please choose a number from the menu.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A dictionary maps menu choices to functions: no long if/elif chain needed, and adding a feature means adding one line.

The complete program

Put all the pieces together in tracker.py in this order: imports, the dataclass, the constants, the functions from steps 2–6, then main(). All the imports at the top:

import csv
import json
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

Run it:

python tracker.py

Add a few expenses, quit, and run it again: your data is still there in expenses.json.

Testing the logic without typing

Functions that don't ask for input are easy to test automatically. Here's a quick check of the reports with sample data:

from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Expense:
    id: int
    day: str
    description: str
    category: str
    amount: float

sample = [
    Expense(1, "2024-05-01", "Lunch", "food", 180),
    Expense(2, "2024-05-02", "Metro card", "transport", 500),
    Expense(3, "2024-05-15", "Groceries", "food", 1450.5),
    Expense(4, "2024-06-01", "Electricity", "bills", 1320),
]

totals = defaultdict(float)
for e in sample:
    totals[e.category] += e.amount
print(dict(totals))   # {'food': 1630.5, 'transport': 500.0, 'bills': 1320.0}

months = defaultdict(float)
for e in sample:
    months[e.day[:7]] += e.amount
print(dict(months))   # {'2024-05': 2130.5, '2024-06': 1320.0}

In a real project, you'd put checks like this in a test file and run them with pytest.

What you used from the course

  • Variables, strings, numbers and f-string formatting.
  • Lists, dictionaries, defaultdict, sorting with key= and lambdas.
  • Loops, conditions and a dictionary of functions.
  • Functions with clear single jobs, and if __name__ == "__main__":.
  • A dataclass, JSON and CSV files, pathlib.
  • Exceptions for invalid input and damaged files.

Ideas to extend it

  • A budget per category with a warning when you go over it.
  • Edit an existing expense.
  • Filter the list by month or category.
  • Store data in SQLite with the built-in sqlite3 module, using what you learned in the SQL course.
  • Draw a real chart with matplotlib (see the pip lesson).
  • Turn it into a small web app with Flask.

Summary

  • Model data with a dataclass and store it as JSON for persistence.
  • Validate every input with loops and exceptions.
  • Keep functions small, and map menu choices to functions with a dictionary.
  • Separate logic from input/output so it can be tested.

Congratulations on finishing the Python course! You can now write useful programs that read, process and save real data. From here, explore web development with Flask or Django, data analysis with pandas, or AI with the guides in our AI section.
item.excerpt:encoded: Build a command-line expense tracker step by step with a dataclass, functions, JSON storage, error handling, reports by category and month, and CSV export.
